topics.title: Propositional logic
topics.subtitle: From statements to clauses, models and refutations.

concepts.title: Syntax & semantics
concepts.body: A valuation assigns each atom 0 or 1. A model of a knowledge base makes every formula true. A formula is valid if every valuation satisfies it; satisfiable if at least one does.

concepts.title: Entailment
concepts.body: KB ⊨ φ iff every model of KB satisfies φ. Test this by checking that KB ∧ ¬φ is unsatisfiable. An inconsistent KB classically entails every formula.

concepts.title: Rewrite to CNF
concepts.body: Remove → using ¬A ∨ B; push negations inward using De Morgan and double negation; distribute ∨ over ∧. CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals.

concepts.title: Resolution
concepts.body: From C ∨ p and D ∨ ¬p infer C ∨ D. Add the negated goal and derive the empty clause □ to prove entailment. Resolving two complementary pairs at once is invalid.

concepts.title: Horn & Datalog by hand
concepts.body: A definite Horn rule has one positive head. Start from facts and repeatedly fire rules whose bodies are true until no new fact is added. This computes the least fixed point for a finite function-free positive program.

concepts.title: Natural deduction & functional completeness
concepts.body: Modus ponens eliminates →; proving A → B means temporarily assuming A and deriving B. NAND is functionally complete: ¬p = p ↑ p and p ∧ q = (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q).

concepts.title: Semantic proof patterns
concepts.body: Entailment ↔ refutation, monotonicity and the deduction property can all be proved by quantifying over valuations. Soundness and completeness compare derivability with entailment; satisfiability concerns one formula or KB.

traps: A satisfiable formula need not be valid.
The converse q → p does not follow from p → q.
A failed proof search alone is not a countermodel.

topics.title: First-order logic
topics.subtitle: Translate carefully, normalize, then reason with witnesses.

concepts.title: Language
concepts.body: Constants name individuals; variables range over a nonempty domain; predicates express relations; functions return individuals. A free variable is not in the scope of a corresponding quantifier.

concepts.title: Quantifier order
concepts.body: ∀x∃y R(x,y) allows y to depend on x. ∃y∀x R(x,y) requires one common witness. The latter entails the former, but the converse generally fails.

concepts.title: Negation & prenex form
concepts.body: ¬∀x φ ≡ ∃x ¬φ and ¬∃x φ ≡ ∀x ¬φ. Rename bound variables before moving quantifiers; the variable moved across a connective must not be free in the other operand.

concepts.title: Skolemization
concepts.body: Replace an existential by a fresh constant if it has no preceding universal dependency, otherwise by a fresh function of those universal variables. Skolemization preserves satisfiability, not logical equivalence in the original signature.

concepts.title: Unification & resolution
concepts.body: Unification finds a substitution making terms identical. Check repeated variables and the occurs check. Standardize clause variables apart before resolution; universally quantified variables are implicit in clauses.

concepts.title: Inference side conditions
concepts.body: ∀ elimination substitutes a term for a universal variable. ∃ introduction gives a witness. In ∃ elimination the temporary witness is fresh and may not escape into a conclusion that depends on its identity.

concepts.title: Interpretations and relational chains
concepts.body: An interpretation supplies a domain, constants, functions and predicate relations. A sentence with linked relations may need several nested witnesses. Clause normalization must respect free variables and witness dependencies.

traps: Do not swap ∀ and ∃.
An existential witness is not automatically a named individual.
P(x,x) and P(a,b) do not unify when a and b are distinct constants.

topics.title: Planning
topics.subtitle: Write actions and transitions instead of implementing a solver.

concepts.title: Classical planning
concepts.body: A state is a set of true ground atoms. Under the closed-world convention, other ground atoms are false. A plan is an applicable action sequence whose final state satisfies the goal.

concepts.title: STRIPS
concepts.body: An action has preconditions Pre(a), add effects Add(a), and delete effects Del(a). It is applicable when Pre(a) ⊆ S. Its successor is γ(S,a)=(S ∖ Del(a)) ∪ Add(a).

concepts.title: Frame problem
concepts.body: Facts unaffected by an action persist. SAT encodings need frame constraints in addition to precondition and effect constraints; otherwise facts can change without a cause.

concepts.title: Planning as SAT
concepts.body: At horizon H introduce state variables p₀,…,pH and action variables a₀,…,aH−1. Encode initial facts, goal at H, action preconditions, effects, persistence and the chosen serial/concurrent action semantics.

concepts.title: Subgoal interaction
concepts.body: Achieving one subgoal may destroy another. Blocks-world examples such as the Sussman anomaly require interleaving; solving each goal once in isolation can fail.

concepts.title: Beyond deterministic planning
concepts.body: The lecture introduces probabilistic transitions p(s′|s,a), rewards, policies and expected discounted return ΣγᵗE[rₜ]. Revise those definitions and small expectation calculations. Belief-state updates and POMDP solution algorithms are not taught in the supplied slides and are not required here.

concepts.title: Subgoal order, invariants and bounds
concepts.body: Trace the Sussman anomaly, justify state invariants from preconditions and effects, and distinguish the first feasible horizon from an arbitrary feasible bound. For stochastic examples compute only the transition/reward expectations introduced in the lecture.

traps: Effects apply only when preconditions hold.
A SAT model at horizon H is not necessarily a shortest plan.
Do not assume concurrent actions unless the encoding allows them.

topics.title: Concepts & association rules
topics.subtitle: Derive extents, intents, lattices and useful rules.

concepts.title: Formal context
concepts.body: A context (G,M,I) consists of objects G, attributes M and incidence I. A′ is the set of attributes shared by all objects in A; B′ is the set of objects having every attribute in B.

concepts.title: Closure
concepts.body: Derivation reverses inclusion. Double derivation is extensive, monotone and idempotent: B ⊆ B″, B ⊆ C ⇒ B″ ⊆ C″, B⁗=B″. The empty intersection convention gives ∅′=M on the object side and ∅′=G on the attribute side.

concepts.title: Formal concept & lattice
concepts.body: (A,B) is a formal concept iff A′=B and B′=A. Order concepts by extent inclusion, equivalently reverse intent inclusion. In a Hasse diagram draw only cover relations, not every comparable pair.

concepts.title: Association rules
concepts.body: support(X⇒Y)=support(X∪Y); confidence(X⇒Y)=support(X∪Y)/support(X); lift=confidence/support(Y). Confidence is undefined if support(X)=0.

concepts.title: Implications & frequent itemsets
concepts.body: An implication X→Y holds when Y ⊆ X″. Unlike an association rule that may tolerate exceptions, an implication holds for every object in the context. Apriori uses support anti-monotonicity: a superset cannot be more frequent than a subset.

concepts.title: Closed and maximal itemsets
concepts.body: A closed itemset has no strict superset with the same support; equivalently X=X″ for the transaction context. A maximal frequent itemset has no frequent strict superset. Closed frequent itemsets preserve more support information than maximal ones.

concepts.title: Meet, join & NextClosure
concepts.body: For concepts (A₁,B₁),(A₂,B₂), meet has extent A₁∩A₂ and intent (B₁∪B₂)″; join has extent (A₁∪A₂)″ and intent B₁∩B₂. NextClosure enumerates closed intents in lectical order, starting at ∅″ and rejecting pivots whose closure introduces a new earlier attribute.

concepts.title: Implication bases & preprocessing
concepts.body: Use Armstrong reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity to reason with implications. A complete nonredundant basis derives all valid implications without dispensable rules. The DG basis uses pseudo-intents. Clarification removes duplicate rows/columns; reduction also removes derivable information. The lattice structure is preserved, but discarding duplicate transactions can change empirical supports.

concepts.title: FP-Growth and lecture overview
concepts.body: FP-Growth counts frequent items, orders each transaction, builds a prefix-count tree, and mines conditional pattern bases/trees. FP-Max targets maximal frequent sets. Alternative FCA algorithms and scaling/iceberg extensions appear as overview topics; detailed implementations are outside this written review.

concepts.title: From slide tables to definitions
concepts.body: Reproduce both lecture contexts and the five market baskets. Match ↑/↓ with prime notation; distinguish closure from maximal frequency, and exact implications from confidence with zero support.

traps: Do not swap extent and intent.
High confidence can reflect a common consequent, not a useful association.
At zero antecedent support, do not divide by zero.

coverage.skill: Support, confidence, lift and rule generation
Apriori, FP-Growth, closed and maximal sets

topics.title: Fuzzy & soft logic
topics.subtitle: Choose an operator, compute its value, explain its meaning.

concepts.title: Truth degree ≠ probability
concepts.body: A fuzzy degree measures graded satisfaction of a vague property. Probability measures uncertainty about whether an event occurs. Combining degrees requires the specified fuzzy operators, not an independence assumption.

concepts.title: Negation & t-norms
concepts.body: With standard negation N(a)=1−a: minimum T=min(a,b), product T=ab, Łukasiewicz T=max(0,a+b−1), drastic T=b if a=1, a if b=1, otherwise 0. A t-norm is associative, commutative, monotone and has neutral element 1.

concepts.title: Dual disjunction
concepts.body: For a chosen t-norm, S(a,b)=1−T(1−a,1−b). This yields max, a+b−ab, min(1,a+b), and the drastic conorm. The maximum t-norm bounds all t-norms from above.

concepts.title: Implications
concepts.body: S-implication uses S(1−a,b). Residual implication is I(a,b)=sup{c:T(a,c)≤b}. They need not agree: under min, S-implication=max(1−a,b), while the residual is 1 if a≤b and b otherwise.

concepts.title: Weighted MAX-SAT
concepts.body: For Boolean assignments, maximize the sum of weights of satisfied clauses. It is an optimization objective, not the probability that all formulas are true. Enumerate small instances on paper.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Soft Logic
concepts.body: Relax atom values to [0,1]. Under Łukasiewicz disjunction, clause truth is min(1,sum of literal truth values). Weighted clause truth maximization is equivalent to minimizing weighted hinge losses max(0,1−sum); with nonnegative weights and linear constraints this formulation is convex.

concepts.title: Optimization by cases
concepts.body: For small relaxed MAX-SAT examples, split at hinge boundaries and optimize the resulting affine pieces. A common positive scaling of weights preserves the maximizers. Distinguish clause weights, fuzzy degrees and event probabilities.

concepts.title: Fuzzy sets and inference systems
concepts.body: Membership functions μ:U→[0,1], support/core/cuts, capping, fuzzy equality, fuzzification and defuzzification lead to the Mamdani rule pipeline. Positive rule inference computes least truth assignments; this differs from evaluating a fixed formula.

traps: Always name the t-norm and implication convention.
Fuzzy p ∨ ¬p need not have degree 1 under every choice.
A Boolean optimum need not equal the relaxed optimum.

coverage.skill: Degree versus probability and weighted clauses
Negation, t-norms, conorms and their axioms
PSL clause truth, hinge losses and relaxation

topics.title: Theorem proving
topics.subtitle: Reduce terms, avoid capture, and connect proofs with types.

concepts.title: Lambda syntax
concepts.body: Terms are variables x, abstractions λx.M and applications M N. Application associates left: f x y=(f x)y. An abstraction extends as far right as parentheses allow.

concepts.title: Alpha & beta
concepts.body: Alpha-conversion consistently renames bound variables. Beta-reduction (λx.M) N → M[x:=N] substitutes only free occurrences of x, renaming bound variables first to avoid capture.

concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.body: A normal form contains no β-redex. Strong normalization means every reduction sequence terminates. Untyped lambda calculus admits divergence; simply typed lambda calculus is strongly normalizing.

concepts.title: Church encodings
concepts.body: n=λf.λx.fⁿx, true=λa.λb.a, false=λa.λb.b. SUCC=λn.λf.λx.f(n f x). Boolean encodings select branches by function application.

concepts.title: Curry–Howard
concepts.body: Propositions correspond to types and proofs to terms. Implication is function type, conjunction product, disjunction sum, truth unit and falsehood empty type. → introduction corresponds to abstraction; → elimination to application.

concepts.title: Constructivity & limits
concepts.body: A constructive existence proof supplies a witness. Classical excluded-middle reasoning may prove existence without selecting a witness. Gödel incompleteness applies to consistent effectively axiomatized theories sufficiently expressive for arithmetic; it is not a failure of propositional completeness. Proof checking and proof discovery are different tasks.

concepts.title: Church data and proof rules
concepts.body: Trace addition, successor, multiplication and boolean encodings using capture-avoiding β-reduction. Read application left-associatively. For natural deduction, label branch assumptions and discharge rules, especially disjunction elimination.

traps: Never capture a free variable during substitution.
The existence of one terminating strategy is weaker than strong normalization.
A proof checker checks a formal statement, which may differ from the intended informal claim.

topics.title: Description logic
topics.subtitle: Read restrictions, construct models and test subsumption.

concepts.title: Vocabulary & semantics
concepts.body: Concepts denote subsets of a nonempty domain; roles denote binary relations; individuals denote domain elements. A TBox specifies concept axioms; an ABox gives individual concept and role assertions.

concepts.title: ALC constructors
concepts.body: (C⊓D)ᴵ=Cᴵ∩Dᴵ, (C⊔D)ᴵ=Cᴵ∪Dᴵ, (¬C)ᴵ=Δᴵ∖Cᴵ. (∃r.C)ᴵ contains elements with at least one r-successor in C; (∀r.C)ᴵ contains elements whose every r-successor is in C.

concepts.title: Vacuity & open world
concepts.body: ∀r.C does not imply an r-successor exists: it is true when there are none. Missing assertions are unknown under open-world reasoning, not automatically false. Different names need not denote distinct individuals without an explicit distinctness assumption.

concepts.title: Reasoning tasks
concepts.body: C⊑D means Cᴵ⊆Dᴵ in every model of the TBox. Concept satisfiability asks whether C can have an instance in some model; consistency asks whether the entire ontology has a model. Reduce subsumption to unsatisfiability of C⊓¬D.

concepts.title: Tableau reasoning
concepts.body: Expand conjunctions, branch on disjunctions, create a witness for an existential, and propagate universals to all matching successors. A branch closes on C and ¬C at the same node. One open complete branch witnesses satisfiability for the relevant calculus.

concepts.title: Ontology languages
concepts.body: DL provides a formal basis for OWL-style ontologies. Cardinality restrictions need explicit semantics: ≥n r.C requires n distinct qualifying successors. Inverse roles reverse edge direction; do not infer symmetry merely from a role name.

concepts.title: Role extensions & cardinality
concepts.body: Qualified cardinalities count distinct successors in a filler concept. Inverse roles reverse edges; transitive roles compose along paths; subroles imply edges in a superrole. Domain and range axioms infer classifications under open-world semantics rather than simply validate an input table.

concepts.title: Ontology and OWL vocabulary
concepts.body: Revise the family TBox/ABox, reasoning services, ontology/KB tuples, rule chaining, OWL constructors and property characteristics. Domain and range produce consequences; they are not automatically validation checks.

traps: A universal restriction is not an existence claim.
Non-entailment is different from entailment of the negation.
A contradictory concept may be empty while the TBox stays consistent.

exercises.title: A knowledge base with no model
exercises.prompt: Let KB = {p ∨ q, p → r, q → r, ¬r}. Prove that KB is unsatisfiable using resolution, then give a semantic argument.
exercises.hint: Replace each implication by a two-literal clause.
steps: The clauses are C₁={p,q}, C₂={¬p,r}, C₃={¬q,r}, C₄={¬r}.
Resolve C₂ with C₄ to obtain {¬p}. Resolve C₃ with C₄ to obtain {¬q}.
Resolve C₁ with {¬p} to obtain {q}; resolve with {¬q} to obtain □.
Semantically, ¬r forces p=false and q=false through the two implications, contradicting p ∨ q.
exercises.origin: Original practice · based on current course concepts

extension.prompt: Show that the KB is minimally unsatisfiable: for each removed formula, give a model of all remaining formulas. Does adding a redundant formula preserve minimal unsatisfiability?
steps: In the original formula order, deletion models (p,q,r) are 000, 100, 010, 111. Each satisfies the other three formulas, so every proper subset is satisfiable.
Adding the redundant formula p∨q∨r keeps the set inconsistent but destroys minimality: deleting that added formula leaves the original inconsistency.
rubric: Four deletion witnesses checked against the remaining KB

exercises.prompt: Convert ¬(p → (q ∧ r)) into equivalent CNF. Give all satisfying assignments.
exercises.hint: Negate ¬p ∨ (q ∧ r), then apply De Morgan.
steps: Negating gives p ∧ ¬(q ∧ r) ≡ p ∧ (¬q ∨ ¬r).
Thus p=1 and q,r are not both 1: (p,q,r)=(1,0,0),(1,0,1),(1,1,0).

extension.prompt: Generalize to Φₙ=¬(p→(q₁∧…∧qₙ)), n≥1. Give a CNF and count its models over exactly these n+1 atoms. Prove that every clause in your CNF is necessary.

exercises.title: One implication, two different claims
exercises.prompt: Does {p → q, q} entail p? Does {p → q, p} entail q? Justify both answers.
exercises.hint: To disprove entailment, make the premises true and the conclusion false.
steps: No for the first claim: p=0,q=1 satisfies p → q and q, but not p.
Yes for the second: modus ponens gives q from p → q and p. Equivalently, adding ¬q produces a contradiction.
Observing q does not establish that p caused it.

extension.prompt: For formulas A,B, determine exactly when {A→B,B} entails A. Express the condition as validity of one implication and as unsatisfiability of one conjunction. Test A=p∧r, B=p.
steps: Because B already makes A→B true, the premise set has exactly the models of B. Hence it entails A iff B→A is valid, equivalently B∧¬A is unsatisfiable.
With A=p∧r and B=p, take p=1,r=0. The premises hold but A fails; the reverse implication p→(p∧r) is not valid.

exercises.title: Follow the least fixed point
exercises.prompt: Facts: Edge(a,b), Edge(b,c), Edge(c,d). Rules: Path(x,y) ← Edge(x,y); Path(x,z) ← Path(x,y) ∧ Edge(y,z). List every derived Path fact, by synchronous rounds.
exercises.hint: In each round, use facts known at the end of the preceding round.
steps: Round 1: Path(a,b), Path(b,c), Path(c,d).
Round 2 adds Path(a,c), Path(b,d). Round 3 adds Path(a,d).
No further paths are added. The six listed facts form the Path relation at the least fixed point; no reverse or reflexive paths follow.
exercises.origin: Original practice · based on current course concepts

extension.prompt: Replace the chain by n vertices v₁→…→vₙ, n≥2. Prove the exact content of round k, the number of rounds that add facts, and the final number of Path facts. Then add vₙ→v₁ and answer the last two questions again.
steps: With round 0 containing no Path facts, after round k the chain contains exactly pairs (vᵢ,vⱼ) with 1≤j−i≤k. Prove by induction using the one-edge extension rule. The final new fact arrives in round n−1; there are n(n−1)/2 facts.

For the directed cycle, round k adds pairs at forward distance k for 1≤k≤n, with distance n giving the diagonal. There are n rounds that add facts and n² final facts. An extra check round detects stability.

exercises.title: Prove a small theorem
exercises.prompt: Give a natural-deduction proof of (p ∧ (p → q)) → q. Label assumptions and discharged assumptions.
exercises.hint: Assume the entire antecedent, then use ∧ elimination twice.
steps: Assume H: p ∧ (p → q).
From H obtain p and p → q by ∧ elimination. Apply → elimination to get q.
Discharge H by → introduction, giving (p ∧ (p → q)) → q.

extension.prompt: Give natural-deduction proofs of ((p→q)∧(q→r))→(p→r) and (p→(q→r))→((p∧q)→r). Label every discharge, then explain why replacing the last conjunction p∧q by p∨q invalidates the second claim.

exercises.title: Build connectives from NAND
exercises.prompt: Using only ↑, express ¬p, p ∧ q and p ∨ q. Here p ↑ q = ¬(p ∧ q).
exercises.hint: Use the same input twice to obtain negation.
steps: ¬p = p ↑ p.
p ∨ q = (p ↑ p) ↑ (q ↑ q), by De Morgan. These constructions show functional completeness because ¬ and ∧ suffice.

extension.prompt: Prove functional completeness by structural induction on formulas built from ¬ and ∧. Then prove that a language using only ∧ and ∨, even with Boolean constants, cannot express ¬p.

Every ∧/∨/constant formula is monotone in each input, by structural induction. Negation decreases from 1 to 0 when p increases from 0 to 1, so it is not expressible in that language.

exercises.title: Find every model
exercises.prompt: For KB={p → q, q → r}, enumerate all models over p,q,r. Is r entailed? Is p → r entailed?
exercises.hint: The truth values must satisfy p ≤ q ≤ r.
steps: Models in (p,q,r) order: 000, 001, 011, 111.
r is not entailed: 000 is a countermodel.
p → r is entailed: if p is true, q and then r must be true; in the remaining models the implication is vacuously true.

extension.prompt: For Kₙ={p₁→p₂,…,pₙ₋₁→pₙ}, n≥2, characterize and count all models. For distinct i,j, determine exactly when Kₙ entails pᵢ→pⱼ and supply a countermodel in every other case.
steps: Models are strings of zero or more zeros followed by zero or more ones. A 1 cannot be followed by a 0 along the chain. There are n+1 possible cut positions.
Entailment holds for i<j by chaining implications. For i>j, choose the cut immediately before i: pᵢ=1 but pⱼ=0, while all chain implications hold.

exercises.title: Every student has an adviser
exercises.prompt: Use Student(x) and Advises(y,x). Formalize “Every student has an adviser.” Negate your formula, and compare it to “Someone advises every student.”
exercises.hint: Advises has adviser first and student second.
steps: ∀x (Student(x) → ∃y Advises(y,x)).
Its negation is ∃x (Student(x) ∧ ∀y ¬Advises(y,x)).
The common-adviser claim is ∃y∀x (Student(x) → Advises(y,x)). It implies the first claim in nonempty domains.
The converse fails with two students and two advisers, each adviser advising only one student.

extension.prompt: Construct a smallest countermodel to the common-adviser converse when advisers may themselves be students. Prove minimality. What happens to both claims when there are no students in a nonempty domain?
steps: Two elements suffice: both are students and Advises={(a,a),(b,b)}. Each student has an adviser, but neither element advises both. One element cannot separate the formulas: if it is a student, its only possible adviser is itself; if it is not, both claims are vacuously satisfied.
With no students, the first universal is true. Since the domain is nonempty, any individual witnesses the second formula, whose inner implication is always true.
rubric: Correct empty-student case with nonempty domain

exercises.title: Make the witness dependency visible
exercises.prompt: Put ∀x (P(x) → ∃y (R(x,y) ∧ Q(y))) into clausal form. Explain why a Skolem constant is generally insufficient.
exercises.hint: The existential witness is selected separately for each x.
steps: Eliminate →: ∀x (¬P(x) ∨ ∃y(R(x,y) ∧ Q(y))).
Move ∃y outward (y is not free in P(x)), then replace y with fresh f(x).
The clauses are {¬P(x),R(x,f(x))} and {¬P(x),Q(f(x))}. Universal quantifiers are implicit.
A constant would force a single witness for all P objects, a stronger requirement. Skolemization is an equisatisfiable signature extension.

Since this holds for each m∈B, B⊆B″. If B′ is empty, all attributes are shared vacuously, so the conclusion still holds.

extension.prompt: Also prove monotonicity and idempotence of double derivation. Deduce that the intersection of any family of closed attribute sets is closed, including the empty family.
steps: Derivation is antitone: B⊆C implies C′⊆B′. Applying it twice gives B″⊆C″. Extensivity for both object and attribute sets yields B′=B‴, hence B″=B⁗, proving idempotence.
For closed Bᵢ and B=∩Bᵢ, monotonicity gives B″⊆Bᵢ″=Bᵢ for every i; hence B″⊆B. Extensivity gives equality. The empty intersection is the full attribute set, which is closed.

exercises.title: Closed is different from maximal
exercises.prompt: Transactions: {a,b}, {a,b}, {a}. Minimum support is 2/3. List frequent nonempty itemsets; identify closed frequent and maximal frequent itemsets.
exercises.hint: Adding b changes the support of a, but adding a does not change the support of b.
steps: Frequent: {a} with support 1; {b} with support 2/3; {a,b} with support 2/3.
Closed frequent: {a} and {a,b}. {b} is not closed because {a,b} has the same support.
Maximal frequent: only {a,b}; {a} is closed but not maximal because it has a frequent strict superset.
Thus closed and maximal are different notions.

extension.prompt: Prove every maximal frequent itemset is closed. Show that closed frequent itemsets with their support counts determine the supports of all frequent itemsets, whereas maximal frequent itemsets alone do not.
steps: If a maximal frequent X were not closed, X″ would be a strict superset with the same support, hence frequent, a contradiction.

For frequent X, X″ is a frequent closed superset with exactly its support; every other closed superset has support no larger. Thus supp(X) is the maximum support among closed supersets. extension.prompt: Add the role conditions seriality (every element has an r-successor) and functionality (at most one r-successor). Determine which condition repairs each failed inclusion. Prove the resulting equivalence when both hold.

exercises.title: Entailment and refutation are the same test
exercises.prompt: Prove KB ⊨ φ iff KB∪{¬φ} has no model. State why this also works when KB itself is inconsistent.
exercises.hint: Negate the condition “every KB-model satisfies φ”.
steps: If KB entails φ, a model of KB∪{¬φ} would satisfy both φ and ¬φ, impossible.
Conversely, if entailment fails, some KB-model falsifies φ; that same valuation satisfies KB∪{¬φ}, contradicting unsatisfiability.
If KB is inconsistent it has no models. Entailment holds vacuously, and adding ¬φ cannot create a model.

extension.prompt: Find a consistent KB that entails φ∨ψ while entailing neither disjunct. Translate all three entailment tests into refutation tests, and identify the invalid inference in treating the disjunction as two separate obligations.

KB∧¬(p∨q)=KB∧¬p∧¬q is unsatisfiable, while KB∧¬p and KB∧¬q are separately satisfiable. Absence of a model falsifying both is not absence of a model falsifying either one.

exercises.title: Use the deduction property
exercises.prompt: Prove KB∪{p} ⊨ q iff KB ⊨ p→q, by valuation semantics.
exercises.hint: Only valuations with p=true can falsify the implication.
steps: Suppose the left side holds. In any KB-model, either p is false, making p→q true, or p is true, in which case q is true by the premise.
For the reverse, any model of KB∪{p} satisfies p→q and p, so q is true.
This is a semantic statement; the proof uses no assumption that KB is consistent.

extension.prompt: Extend the deduction property to premises p₁,…,pₙ. Prove the equivalence between the resulting implication and its curried form p₁→(p₂→…(pₙ→q)). Explain the n=0 case.
steps: KB∪{p₁,…,pₙ}⊨q iff KB⊨(p₁∧…∧pₙ)→q: a countermodel in either formulation satisfies KB and every pᵢ but falsifies q.
The curried formula has exactly the same falsifying valuations: every antecedent true, q false. With no added premises the conjunction is ⊤ and the test reduces to KB⊨q.

exercises.title: Monotonicity and explosion
exercises.prompt: Prove: if KB ⊨ φ then KB∪{ψ} ⊨ φ. Also explain why {p,¬p} entails q, even if p and q are unrelated.
exercises.hint: Adding assumptions can only remove models.
steps: Every model of KB∪{ψ} is a KB-model, so it satisfies φ.
No valuation satisfies both p and ¬p, so there is no countermodel to q. This is classical explosion by vacuous universal quantification over models.
Explosion is not evidence that q is true in the actual world; it identifies the consequences of an inconsistent classical premise set.

extension.prompt: Let K={p→q,p,¬q}. List all inclusion-maximal consistent subsets. Which of p,q,¬p,¬q is entailed by every such subset? Compare this with consequence from K itself.
steps: The maximal consistent subsets are {p→q,p}, {p→q,¬q}, and {p,¬q}; every pair is satisfiable and adding the missing formula is inconsistent.

steps: Set v(p),v(q) on atoms; v(¬A)=1−v(A); v(A∧B)=min(v(A),v(B)); v(A∨B)=max(v(A),v(B)); v(A→B)=max(1−v(A),v(B)) for Boolean values.
Here p∨q=1, ¬q=1, p∧¬q=1.

extension.prompt: Prove by structural induction that valuations agreeing on all atoms occurring in φ give the same value to φ. Use this to count the models of your displayed formula over {p,q,r₁,…,rₖ} without a full truth table.
steps: For an atom the agreement is given. Each connective computes its value solely from its immediate subformulas, so the induction hypothesis propagates agreement through ¬,∧,∨,→.

exercises.title: Explain soundness and completeness
exercises.prompt: What do soundness and completeness of a propositional proof calculus mean? Distinguish them from satisfiability and consistency of one knowledge base.
exercises.hint: One property concerns what proofs establish; the other what semantic consequences can be proved.
steps: Soundness: KB⊢φ implies KB⊨φ. The calculus proves only semantic consequences.
Completeness: KB⊨φ implies KB⊢φ. It can prove every semantic consequence.
Satisfiability/semantic consistency asks whether one KB has a model; it is not a property of all inference rules.

extension.prompt: Consider a calculus whose only derivations are assumptions and repeated modus ponens, with no axioms. Prove soundness and exhibit incompleteness. Then add the rule ‘from A∨B infer A’; prove that soundness fails.
steps: Induct on derivation length: assumptions hold in any premise model, and a true A with true A→B forces B. Yet with no premises this calculus derives nothing, so it cannot prove the valid p→p.
The added rule fails on p∨q with valuation p=0,q=1. It derives a false conclusion from a true premise. One countervaluation suffices to refute soundness.

steps: Rename the second bound x to z: (∀x P(x))∨(∃z Q(z,y)).
A prenex form is ∀x∃z (P(x)∨Q(z,y)), over the course’s nonempty domains. x is not free in Q(z,y), and z is not free in P(x).

exercises.prompt: Given ∃x P(x) and ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)), prove ∃x Q(x) by natural deduction. What would be wrong with concluding Q(ada)?
exercises.hint: Introduce a fresh temporary witness c inside a subproof.
steps: Assume P(c) for fresh c as the existential witness. Instantiate the universal to get P(c)→Q(c), then infer Q(c).
Introduce ∃x Q(x), and discharge the witness subproof. c does not occur free in that conclusion or in undischarged assumptions outside its scope.
Q(ada) is not justified: the existing witness need not denote Ada.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Prove ∃x(P(x)∧Q(x)) from the original premises, respecting the witness condition. Then determine whether {∃x P(x),∃x Q(x)} alone entails that same conclusion; give a smallest countermodel if not.
steps: Inside the fresh-c subproof, derive Q(c), combine with P(c), then introduce ∃x(P(x)∧Q(x)) before discharging the witness. The conclusion contains no free c.
Separate existence does not suffice: domain {a,b}, P={a}, Q={b}. One-element models with both existential premises must overlap, so size two is minimal.

exercises.title: Everyone knows someone is not everyone knows everyone
exercises.prompt: Compare ∀x∃y Knows(x,y) and ∀x∀y Knows(x,y). Give a model satisfying the first but not the second. Negate the second.
exercises.hint: A two-person model with only self-knowledge suffices.
steps: Domain={a,b}, Knows={(a,a),(b,b)} satisfies the first formula.
The second is false because Knows(a,b) is false. It is strictly stronger.
Its negation is ∃x∃y ¬Knows(x,y), witnessed by (a,b).

extension.prompt: Over nonempty domains compare A=∀x∃y R(x,y), B=∃y∀x R(x,y), and C=∀x∀y R(x,y). Give all implications among them and smallest countermodels to their converses.
steps: C implies B by selecting any domain element, and B implies A by using its common witness for each x; consequently C implies A.

A does not imply B: two-element identity relation. B does not imply C: on {a,b}, use R={(a,a),(b,a)}. Both also show failure of weaker-to-stronger implications as appropriate; A not⇒C follows from identity. No one-element countermodel exists because all three reduce to the single self-edge.

exercises.title: Translate a relational chain
exercises.prompt: Use Student(x), Course(y), Teacher(z), Takes(x,y) and Teaches(z,y). Formalize “Every student takes a course taught by a teacher.” Negate the formula. Do not require one common course or teacher.

steps: ∀x(Student(x)→∃y∃z(Course(y)∧Teacher(z)∧Takes(x,y)∧Teaches(z,y))).
Its negation is ∃x(Student(x)∧∀y∀z(¬Course(y)∨¬Teacher(z)∨¬Takes(x,y)∨¬Teaches(z,y))).
The existential witnesses are inside the scope of ∀x. Pulling them before ∀x would impose shared witnesses that the sentence does not require.

extension.prompt: Skolemize your formalization into separate clauses. Then refute it together with Student(ada) and ∀x∀y∀z((Takes(x,y)∧Teaches(z,y))→¬Teacher(z)).

exercises.title: The Sussman anomaly on three blocks
exercises.prompt: Initially On(C,A), On(A,Table), On(B,Table), with C and B clear. Goal: On(A,B)∧On(B,C). Assume standard clear-block moves. Give a plan, and explain why completing On(A,B) first can interfere with the other goal.
exercises.hint: You must clear A and keep B clear until it can move onto C.
steps: Move C from A to Table; move B from Table to C; move A from Table to B. The goal then holds.
If A is placed onto B before moving B onto C, B is no longer clear and cannot move. Achieving the second goal requires temporarily undoing the first.
The need to coordinate subgoal order/interleaving is the point; the hand-traced solution uses no solver-specific implementation.

steps: C must move off A, B must move onto C, and A must move onto B, giving a lower bound of three attained by the original plan.
Under the imposed order, A must go onto B, off B so B can move, and back onto B: at least three A moves, plus C and B moves. The sequence C→Table, A→B, A→Table, B→C, A→B attains five.
rubric: Order-constrained lower bound and matching witness

exercises.title: Serial actions and mutual exclusion
exercises.prompt: At each of three steps, actions Open,Go,Close are possible. Write an at-most-one-action constraint for one step. How does it differ from exactly one?
exercises.hint: At-most-one forbids all three distinct pairs, but permits all-false.
steps: At time t use (¬Open_t∨¬Go_t)∧(¬Open_t∨¬Close_t)∧(¬Go_t∨¬Close_t).
Exactly one adds Open_t∨Go_t∨Close_t. At-most-one alone permits an idle step.
Idle steps preserve state through frame constraints; permitting several actions requires explicit noninterference/concurrency semantics rather than simply removing all mutex constraints.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Generalize the pairwise at-most-one encoding to k actions and count its clauses. Give a satisfying assignment showing why at-most-one permits idling. Finally, use a precondition/delete conflict to show why merely removing mutex clauses does not define sound parallel execution.
steps: For every i<j add ¬aᵢ,t∨¬aⱼ,t: k(k−1)/2 binary clauses. Exactly-one additionally needs the single k-literal disjunction. Setting every action false satisfies at-most-one.

Let both a,b require p, with a deleting p. Both preconditions can hold in the initial state, yet the order a then b is illegal. A parallel semantics that requires noninterference must exclude this pair; it cannot be obtained just by deleting all mutexes.
rubric: Conflict example tied to an explicit concurrency convention

exercises.title: Prove an invariant is preserved
exercises.prompt: Suppose every legal state has exactly one robot location. Move(u,v), u≠v, requires At(u), deletes At(u), and adds At(v). Prove that this invariant is preserved by an applicable move.
exercises.hint: Use the invariant in the pre-state, not only the effect list.
steps: The precondition and invariant imply At(u) is the unique true location; all other At facts, including At(v), are false.
Deleting At(u) removes that one location. Adding At(v) creates exactly one new location. Unrelated location facts remain false.
Thus the successor again has exactly one location. This argument depends on complete delete/add effects and the legal initial-state invariant.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Suppose two moves Move(u,v) and Move(u,w), with distinct u,v,w, execute together using the union of their effects. Show the location invariant can fail. State a sufficient action-compatibility condition that prevents this case.
steps: Both preconditions hold when the robot is at u. The joint effects delete At(u) and add both At(v),At(w), producing two locations.

Serial at-most-one action prevents the problem. More generally forbid action pairs whose delete effects intersect the other’s preconditions or add effects; these two moves conflict because each deletes the other’s required At(u).
rubric: Explicit reachable prestate and illegal joint poststate
Sufficient compatibility condition applied to the pair

exercises.title: What SATPLAN minimizes
exercises.prompt: A solver finds a horizon-5 plan. Under what search procedure can you conclude it is shortest? What is the relationship between horizon and action count when idle steps are permitted?
exercises.hint: Distinguish a feasible bound from the first feasible bound.
steps: If every smaller horizon 0,…,4 was proven UNSAT under the same serial semantics, 5 is the minimum feasible horizon.
A lone SAT result at H=5 proves feasibility only; shorter plans might exist.
With idle steps, the horizon is an upper bound on serial action count. A returned horizon-5 model may use fewer than five non-idle actions; count the actions and remove idle steps.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: In a deterministic model with at most one action per step and correct idle persistence, prove SAT(H) iff some plan has at most H actions. Deduce what a first satisfiable horizon H says about the number of non-idle actions in its model.
steps: An H-step model gives a legal action sequence after deleting idle steps, of length at most H. Conversely pad any shorter legal plan with idle steps to obtain an H-step model.

If all horizons below H are unsatisfiable, a satisfying model cannot contain an idle step: removing it would yield a plan with fewer than H actions, contradicting minimality. Thus its non-idle action count is exactly H.
rubric: Minimal-horizon contradiction rules out idle steps

exercises.title: Discounted rewards by hand
exercises.prompt: Two deterministic policies have reward streams A:(4,0,0,…) and B:(0,6,0,…). Compare their returns at γ=0.5 and γ=0.9.
exercises.hint: Use G=Σ γᵗr_t, starting at t=0.
steps: At γ=0.5, G_A=4 and G_B=0+0.5×6=3, so A is better.
At γ=0.9, G_A=4 and G_B=5.4, so B is better.
The choice depends on discounting: a higher γ places more relative value on delayed reward. This uses only the lecture’s return objective.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: For 0≤γ<1, derive the full preference regions for A and B, including a tie. Now compare both with C=(1,1,1,…) and determine which of A,B,C is best for every γ.
steps: A and B tie at γ=2/3; A is better below, B above. C has return 1/(1−γ), so C=A at γ=3/4.

B=C solves 6γ(1−γ)=1, with roots (3−√3)/6 and (3+√3)/6. Combining comparisons, A is best for γ<2/3; B for 2/3<γ<(3+√3)/6; C above that upper root. There are A/B and B/C ties at the two switching points; the lower B/C tie is below A.
rubric: Correct upper envelope rather than pairwise ties alone

exercises.title: Expected one-step reward
exercises.prompt: Action a leads to reward 10 with probability 0.3 and 0 otherwise. Action b gives reward 2 certainly. Which maximizes expected immediate reward? Does this alone determine the best infinite-horizon policy?
exercises.hint: Calculate the expectation, then ask what future states might matter.
steps: E[r|a]=0.3×10+0.7×0=3. E[r|b]=2. Action a has the larger expected immediate reward.
This does not settle infinite-horizon choice: future rewards depend on successor states and subsequent actions, discounted by γ.
Without those transitions and future rewards, an optimal long-run policy cannot be identified.

extension.prompt: Fix γ=0.9. Construct two fully specified two-step reward models with the given immediate rewards, one where a is optimal and another where b is optimal. Explain why identical first-step expectations do not imply the same optimal action.
steps: Model I ends after the first reward, so a has expected return 3 versus b’s 2. Equivalently all second-step rewards are zero.

Model II gives a a second reward −10 with certainty, independent of its first outcome, while b’s second reward is 0; the process then ends. Returns are 3−9=−6 and 2, so b is optimal. Immediate reward distributions are unchanged; future consequences reverse the ranking.
rubric: Two complete models preserving the stated first-step distribution

exercises.title: NextClosure with an explicit lectical order
exercises.prompt: Context: 1:{a,b}, 2:{a,c}, 3:{a,b,c}; order a<b<c. Start at ∅″. To find the next intent, scan i from c back to a, close (A∩{j:j<i})∪{i}, and accept only if no earlier attribute absent from A is introduced. List the intents and the first two accepted pivots.
exercises.hint: The starting closure is {a}, not ∅.
steps: ∅″={a}. From A={a}, try pivot c: close {a,c}={a,c}; no earlier new attribute appears, so accept.
From A={a,c}, skip c because c∈A; pivot b gives closure {a,b}. It adds no earlier attribute beyond a, so accept.
From A={a,b}, pivot c yields {a,b,c}. No further pivot is possible. Sequence: {a}, {a,c}, {a,b}, {a,b,c}.
Lectical order is not set inclusion order; the middle intents are incomparable.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Prove the closure operator does not depend on attribute order, although NextClosure’s enumeration does. Recompute the sequence with order c<b<a. Is any candidate pivot rejected during this particular enumeration? Distinguish rejection from skipping a pivot already in the current intent.
steps: Closure uses incidence alone, so relabelling the scan order does not change B′ or B″. With c<b<a the sequence is a,ab,ac,abc.

Starting at a, skip a and accept b, giving ab. From ab, skip a and b and accept c with closure ac. From ac, skip a and accept b, giving abc. There are no rejected candidate pivots in this context; skipping an attribute already present is not a rejected closure test.
rubric: Order-independent closure and correct reverse enumeration
Complete pivot trace distinguishes skips from rejections

exercises.title: Meet and join in a concept lattice
exercises.prompt: In context 1:{a,b}, 2:{a,c}, 3:{a,b,c}, take C=({1,3},{a,b}) and D=({2,3},{a,c}). Compute their meet and join under extent inclusion.
exercises.hint: Meet intersects extents; join closes the union of extents.
steps: Meet extent={1,3}∩{2,3}={3}; its intent is {a,b,c}. Hence C∧D=({3},{a,b,c}).
Intent order is reversed: meet closes the union of intents, while join intersects intents.

extension.prompt: Prove the general meet and join formulas for concepts ordered by extent inclusion, rather than merely applying them. Give a context where the raw union of two extents is not closed.
steps: Intersections of closed extents are closed. Their intersection is contained in both and contains every common lower bound, so it is the meet extent. The closure of their union is the least closed set containing both, so it is the join extent.
Take rows 1:a, 2:b, 3:∅ over attributes {a,b}. The extents {1} and {2} are closed, but {1,2}′=∅ and {1,2}″={1,2,3}; the raw union is not an extent. Closing it is essential.

exercises.title: A tiny canonical implication basis
exercises.prompt: Context over attributes {a,b}: object 1 has {a}, object 2 has {a,b}. Find the closed sets and a complete nonredundant implication basis. Explain why ∅ is the only pseudo-intent here (using: P≠P″ and every smaller pseudo-intent Q⊂P has Q″⊆P).
exercises.hint: All objects share a; compute all four closures.
steps: Closures: ∅″={a}, {a}″={a}, {b}″={a,b}, {a,b}″={a,b}. Closed sets are {a} and {a,b}.
∅ is non-closed and has no smaller pseudo-intent, so it is a pseudo-intent. {b} is not: ∅⊂{b} but ∅″={a} is not a subset of {b}.
The DG basis is ∅→{a}. It yields every closure by adding a and is nonredundant; deleting it loses a valid implication.

extension.prompt: Replace the context by 1:ab,2:ac,3:a over {a,b,c}. Determine every pseudo-intent from the given recursive definition and derive its canonical implication basis.
steps: Closed sets are a,ab,ac,abc; ∅ closes to a and is a pseudo-intent. Any set missing a and strictly containing ∅ fails the pseudo-intent condition because ∅″={a} is not contained in it.
Every set containing a is already closed. Therefore ∅ is the only pseudo-intent and the basis is again ∅→a. Exhausting these two classes proves completeness.

exercises.prompt: Context rows: 1:{a,b}, 2:{a,b}, 3:{a,c}. Identify duplicate rows and columns and give a clarified context. What structural property is preserved?

Pair-to-singleton confidences are (2/5)/(3/5)=2/3; singleton-to-pair confidences are (2/5)/(4/5)=1/2. None reaches 0.75.

exercises.title: Prove the largest t-norm bound
exercises.prompt: Using t-norm monotonicity and the neutral element, prove T(a,b)≤min(a,b), and deduce T(a,1−a)≤0.5.
exercises.hint: Compare b with 1, and a with 1.
steps: Because b≤1, T(a,b)≤T(a,1)=a. Likewise T(a,b)≤T(1,b)=b, using commutativity and neutrality.
Therefore T(a,b)≤min(a,b).
Set b=1−a. The maximum of min(a,1−a) on [0,1] is 0.5, so the weak contradiction bound follows.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Prove that any idempotent t-norm, meaning T(a,a)=a for all a, must be minimum. Then find the maximum possible value of T(a,1−a) separately for minimum, product, Łukasiewicz and drastic t-norms.
steps: If a≤b, monotonicity gives a=T(a,a)≤T(a,b)≤T(a,1)=a. Hence T(a,b)=a=min(a,b), with the other order handled by symmetry.
For minimum the maximum is 1/2 at a=1/2. For product, a(1−a)=1/4−(a−1/2)² has maximum 1/4. Łukasiewicz and drastic both give zero for all a in this complementary-input family.
rubric: Four sharp maxima and equality cases

exercises.prompt: Compute residual implications at a=0.8,b=0.3 for product and Łukasiewicz t-norms using I(a,b)=sup{c:T(a,c)≤b}. Do not assume S-implication.

exercises.title: Test classical laws under fuzzy operators
exercises.prompt: At a=0.4 compute a∨¬a and a∧¬a with minimum/max operators and with Łukasiewicz operators. Which classical equalities survive in these examples?

extension.prompt: Test distributivity T(a,S(b,c))=S(T(a,b),T(a,c)) for min/max and Łukasiewicz operators. Prove the min/max case and give an exact Łukasiewicz counterexample. Explain why excluded middle alone does not recover all Boolean algebra laws.

exercises.title: Write the full PSL objective
exercises.prompt: Atoms p,q∈[0,1]. Weighted clauses: p [2], ¬p∨q [3], ¬q [1]. Write the weighted truth objective and equivalent hinge-loss objective. Evaluate both at p=0.7,q=0.4.

steps: Maximize 2p+3min(1,1−p+q)+(1−q). Equivalently minimize 2(1−p)+3max(0,p−q)+q.
At the given point, truth objective=1.4+3×0.7+0.6=4.1. Loss=0.6+0.9+0.4=1.9.
The objectives sum to total weight 6. Nonnegative weighted hinge losses are convex; maximizing the concave truth sum over the box is equivalent.

extension.prompt: Introduce one auxiliary variable u and formulate the hinge-loss minimization as a linear program. Prove equivalence in both directions and give a feasible point attaining loss 1 with a matching lower bound.

exercises.title: Weights are priorities, not probabilities
exercises.prompt: What does multiplying all positive clause weights by 10 do to a weighted MAX-SAT maximizer? Does a weight of 0.8 mean the corresponding formula is true with probability 0.8?
exercises.hint: A common positive scale changes scores but not their order.
steps: All assignment scores are multiplied by 10, so maximizers are unchanged.
A clause weight specifies its contribution to the optimization objective. It is not itself a calibrated event probability.
Probabilistic soft logic combines weighted formulas and fuzzy-valued atoms, but neither interpretation licenses treating every weight as a probability.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Does adding the same positive constant to every clause weight also preserve maximizers? Give a counterexample using only p,q and four distinct clauses. Explain why scaling and translation differ.
steps: Use p [6], ¬p [1], ¬p∨q [1], ¬p∨¬q [1]. Every assignment with p=1 scores 7 and satisfies two clauses; every assignment with p=0 scores 3 and satisfies three clauses. Thus p=1 is initially optimal.

Add 5 to every weight. Assignments with p=1 now score 11+6=17; those with p=0 score 6+6+6=18. The preferred p value reverses. Translation adds c times the number of satisfied clauses, which depends on the assignment; positive scaling multiplies all scores by the same factor.
rubric: Four distinct clauses with original and modified scores
Correct explanation of translation versus scaling

exercises.title: Free and bound occurrences
exercises.prompt: In λx.(x (λy.x y) z), identify free variables, identify the bound occurrences of x and y, and alpha-rename the outer binder to u.
exercises.hint: z is not bound by either lambda.
steps: FV={z}. Both x occurrences are bound by the outer λx; the y occurrence is bound by λy.
Renaming gives λu.(u (λy.u y) z), with fresh u.
The free z remains unchanged; renaming only a binder without its bound occurrences would change the term.

extension.prompt: Infer the most general simple type of the original term, treating z as free, or prove that no such type exists. Contrast with λx.λy.x y, which omits the self-use of x.
steps: Write type(x)=α. The inner application x y forces α=β→γ for type(y)=β, so λy.x y has type β→γ=α. The outer application x (λy.x y) then requires β=α, yielding α=α→γ, impossible for finite simple types.
The simpler term is typable: λx.λy.x y has type (A→B)→A→B. Its argument y is not itself forced to have x’s whole function type.

exercises.title: Read application associativity
exercises.prompt: Reduce ((λx.λy.x) a) b and compare with (λx.λy.x)(a b).
exercises.hint: Application associates left unless parentheses say otherwise.
steps: ((λx.λy.x) a) b→(λy.a)b→a, assuming y is chosen fresh for a.
(λx.λy.x)(a b)→λy.(a b), with capture-avoiding renaming if needed.
The second expression supplies one argument, namely a b; the first supplies a and then b.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: Classify ((λx.λy.x) a) b and (λx.λy.x)(a b) when a,b are arbitrary lambda terms. Must both normalize if a normalizes? Give a counterexample and explain how unused arguments affect normal-order reduction.
steps: The first reduces to a regardless of b. The second reduces to λy.a b with fresh y, so normalization depends on the application a b, not just on a alone.

Take a=λu.u u and b=λu.u u. Each is already in normal form. The first expression normalizes to a; the second becomes λy.Ω and has no β-normal form. Normal-order reduction can discard an unused argument but cannot discard the body of the surviving abstraction.

exercises.title: Church multiplication
exercises.prompt: Let TWO=λf.λx.f(f x), THREE=λf.λx.f(f(f x)), and MUL=λm.λn.λf.λx.m(n f)x. Show MUL TWO THREE represents six.
exercises.hint: THREE f is a function applying f three times.
steps: MUL TWO THREE→λf.λx.TWO(THREE f)x.
TWO(THREE f)x applies THREE f twice, yielding (THREE f)((THREE f)x).
After expanding both uses, the normal form is λf.λx.f(f(f(f(f(f x))))), the Church numeral six.

extension.prompt: Prove MUL M N represents mn for arbitrary Church numerals. Show that the swapped expression MUL N M has the same normal form, and explain why swapping arbitrary lambda terms in this way need not preserve meaning.
steps: N f applies f n times. Iterating N f exactly m times applies f mn times, so MUL M N→*λf.λx.f^(mn)x. The swapped version yields f^(nm)x, identical because integer multiplication commutes.
This relies on numeral structure. For arbitrary m=λu.λv.a and n=λu.λv.b, with distinct free a,b, MUL m n normalizes to λf.λx.a, while MUL n m normalizes to λf.λx.b.

TRUE returns its first argument and FALSE returns its second. With these encodings AND implements conjunction.

extension.prompt: Construct a Church-Boolean XOR term using only TRUE,FALSE and application, then prove its four cases by reduction. Define EVEN on Church numerals using Boolean iteration and prove it tests parity.

exercises.title: Construct conjunction and disjunction proofs
exercises.prompt: Prove (A∧B)→(B∧A). Then prove (A∨B)→(B∨A) using disjunction elimination.

extension.prompt: Prove (A∧(B∨C))→((A∧B)∨(A∧C)) using explicit branches, and prove its converse. In each ∨ elimination identify the common conclusion and discharged assumptions.

exercises.title: Why excluded middle matters to this existence proof
exercises.prompt: Let x=(√2)^(√2). Explain the classical proof that irrational a,b exist with a^b rational, and why this proof does not select one of its two candidate witnesses constructively.
exercises.hint: Split on whether x is rational; do not claim that x is known rational.
steps: If x is rational choose a=b=√2; their power is x.
Otherwise choose a=x and b=√2. Both are irrational and a^b=(√2)^2=2.
This proof uses excluded middle on x being rational but does not decide that case. It establishes existence without selecting the corresponding pair by this argument alone.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: As a witness-construction comparison, take a=√2 and b=log₂9 (the real number satisfying 2ᵇ=9). Prove that both are irrational and that aᵇ=3, using integer prime divisibility and exponent laws. Compare this explicit pair with the earlier undecided case split.
steps: If √2=m/n in lowest positive terms, m²=2n² makes m even; substituting m=2k then makes n even, contradicting coprimality. Thus a is irrational.
If log₂9=m/n were rational in lowest terms with positive integers m,n, then 2^m=9^n=3^(2n), impossible because one side is even and the other odd. Thus b is irrational, as is a=√2.
(√2)^(log₂9)=9^(1/2)=3. This names one pair without deciding the rationality of (√2)^(√2); the explicit witness removes the undecided case split.

exercises.title: Incompleteness is not unsoundness
exercises.prompt: State the relevant limits of a consistent effectively axiomatized theory strong enough for arithmetic. Explain why those limits do not stop a proof assistant from checking a supplied finite proof.
exercises.hint: Separate all true statements from each finite derivation.
steps: Under the first incompleteness theorem’s conditions, the theory cannot prove every arithmetical truth; some statement is undecidable in the theory.

The second theorem, under its standard derivability conditions, prevents a consistent such theory from proving its own formalized consistency. These are not claims that every logic is incomplete or that the theory is inconsistent.
A kernel can still check each supplied finite proof by mechanical rules; incompleteness limits what can be proved, not the verification of a valid derivation.
exercises.origin: Original practice · mapped to current lecture

extension.prompt: A student proposes: ‘Enumerate all finite strings, check which are proofs, and answer NO if a proof of φ has not appeared yet.’ Identify the precise error. What changes if proofs of both φ and ¬φ are searched in parallel, and under which additional condition would this procedure decide every sentence?
steps: At any finite stage, absence of a discovered proof gives no bound on the length of an undiscovered proof. Enumeration can confirm a proof when one appears, but cannot justify NO merely from delay.

Parallel searches terminate for φ exactly when the theory proves φ or ¬φ. They decide all sentences if the theory is syntactically complete and effectively enumerable, with consistency ensuring no conflicting answers. Incompleteness prevents that combination for the sufficiently strong arithmetic theories in the question.
rubric: Failure of the finite-search negative conclusion
Termination condition and role of consistency/completeness

exercises.title: Odd closed walks: a hidden distinction
exercises.prompt: Using only positive Datalog rules, define Odd(x,y) and Even(x,y) for directed paths of positive odd/even length. Test the graph a→b→c→a together with c→d→c. Prove that Odd(d,d) follows although d lies on no odd simple directed cycle. Explain what your rules actually recognize.
exercises.hint: Start Odd with each edge. Extend a path by one edge to reverse its parity. A closed walk may revisit a vertex.
steps: Use Edge(x,y)→Odd(x,y), Odd(x,y)∧Edge(y,z)→Even(x,z), and Even(x,y)∧Edge(y,z)→Odd(x,z). All head variables occur in their bodies.
Induct on path length: the base has length 1 and every extension flips parity. Conversely, every derived fact describes a path of the claimed positive parity; even paths begin at length 2.
At d, the walk d→c→a→b→c→d has length 5, so Odd(d,d) is derived.
Every simple cycle through d must use d→c and c→d, hence is the length-2 cycle. Taking the triangle as a detour revisits c, so it is not simple.
The diagonal query recognizes odd closed walks, not membership in an odd simple cycle. These rules track parity and reachability without testing that all visited vertices are distinct.
rubric: No odd simple cycle through d

extension.prompt: Prove the following characterization for any finite directed graph: Odd(v,v) holds iff v can reach, and be reached from, some odd simple directed cycle. Then prove that if an odd closed walk exists at v in an n-vertex graph, one exists of length at most 2n−1. State explicitly how you handle zero-length connector walks.
steps: Every closed walk decomposes into simple directed cycles by splitting at repeated vertices. If its length is odd, at least one component cycle is odd. Every vertex on that component is mutually reachable with v along the original closed walk.

Conversely choose paths v→u and u→v for a vertex u on an odd cycle. Their concatenation is closed; traversing the odd cycle once between them flips its parity. One of the two walks is odd. Connector paths may have length zero; the chosen odd walk still has positive length.

Record along a shortest odd closed walk the pair (current vertex, parity of elapsed length). A repeated pair would enclose an even-length segment; deleting that segment preserves endpoints and odd parity, contradicting minimality. Start (v,0) and finish (v,1) differ, so at most 2n distinct pairs occur, giving length at most 2n−1.

exercises.title: Why a least model exists
exercises.prompt: Treat a finite ground positive Datalog program as implications A₁∧…∧Aₖ→B, including facts with empty bodies. Prove that the intersection of any nonempty family of its models is also a model. Deduce existence of a least model. Show with a two-atom example why replacing a Horn head by a disjunction can break this argument.
exercises.hint: If every body atom survives the intersection, it is true in every original model.
steps: Let M be the intersection. If a rule body is true in M, each body atom is true in every Mᵢ. Because each Mᵢ satisfies the rule, B belongs to every Mᵢ, hence to M. Facts likewise belong to all models.
The valuation making every atom true is a model of a positive program, so the family of all models is nonempty. Its intersection is a model contained in every other model: the least model.
For p∨q, the models {p} and {q} have intersection ∅, which does not satisfy p∨q.

Thus the unique positive head is essential to this intersection proof; the proof concerns sets of ground facts over a fixed vocabulary/domain, not arbitrary intersections of unrelated first-order domains.
exercises.scope: Datalog theoretical handout: minimal model; propositional implication semantics.
exercises.origin: Original challenge · course and lab concepts only

extension.prompt: Let U be a finite atom set and F a family of subsets of U. Prove that F is exactly the model family of some positive ground Horn program iff U∈F and F is closed under intersections. Construct such a program from F. Also prove that synchronous forward chaining stabilizes after at most |U| rounds that add facts, and exhibit a family attaining that bound.
steps: Necessity follows from the all-true model and intersection closure. For sufficiency define cl(X)=∩{M∈F:X⊆M}; the family in the intersection is nonempty because U∈F, and closure under intersections puts cl(X) in F.

For every X⊆U and every b∈cl(X)∖X add the rule ∧X→b. Each M∈F satisfies every rule: when X⊆M, cl(X)⊆M. If X∉F, then cl(X)≠X and at least one such rule is violated by X. Thus the program’s model family is exactly F. Empty X gives facts.

Start forward chaining from ∅ and derive rule heads using the previous round. A strict round adds at least one previously absent atom, hence there are at most |U| such rounds; a non-strict round is already fixed. The program p₁, p₁→p₂,…,pₙ₋₁→pₙ takes n strict rounds.
rubric: Necessary conditions stated including all-true model

exercises.title: Find the smallest model
exercises.prompt: Consider ∀x∃y R(x,y), ∀x¬R(x,x), and ∀x∀y(R(x,y)→¬R(y,x)), over a nonempty domain. Find the smallest possible finite domain and an interpretation. Then add ∀x∀y∀z((R(x,y)∧R(y,z))→R(x,z)); prove that your smallest model can no longer work. Do not invoke a graph algorithm.
exercises.hint: Every individual needs an outgoing edge, self-loops are forbidden, and an edge rules out its reverse.
steps: A one-element domain fails because the required edge is a forbidden self-loop. In a two-element domain, the only possible outgoing edges are a→b and b→a; requiring both contradicts the third axiom.
Three elements suffice: R={(a,b),(b,c),(c,a)}. Each object has a successor, no self-loop exists, and no edge is accompanied by its reverse.

With transitivity, R(a,b) and R(b,c) force R(a,c), contradicting R(c,a) and asymmetry. More generally every admissible three-element model must give each vertex its only permitted cyclic arrangement, so none can meet the added condition.
The argument establishes the stated minimum and rules out three-element transitive models; it does not infer global inconsistency merely from one failed finite size.
exercises.scope: First-order model construction, quantified axioms and semantic countermodels.

extension.prompt: Classify all possible finite domain sizes for the original three axioms. With transitivity added, prove that no finite model of any size exists, but construct an infinite model. The proof must distinguish absence of finite models from inconsistency.
steps: The possible finite sizes are exactly n≥3. Exclusion of 1 and 2 was proved above; for every n≥3 the directed simple n-cycle is serial, irreflexive and asymmetric.

In a hypothetical finite transitive model, repeatedly choose successors. Some element repeats, giving a positive closed path. Transitivity along the path forces R(x,x), contradicting irreflexivity. This rules out every finite size, not just 3.

On the natural numbers let R(x,y) mean x<y. A successor exists (x+1), and the relation is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive. Hence the strengthened theory is satisfiable but has no finite models.
rubric: Repeated-successor proof for arbitrary finite domains

exercises.title: Witnesses that force a contradiction
exercises.prompt: Refute the following KB using clausal resolution: (1) ∀x(P(x)→∃y(R(x,y)∧P(y))); (2) ∀x∀y(R(x,y)→(Q(x)∨Q(y))); (3) ∃x P(x); (4) ∀x(P(x)→¬Q(x)). Show the Skolem dependencies and every nontrivial substitution.
exercises.hint: The existential root and its generated successor both satisfy P, hence neither can satisfy Q.
steps: Skolemize (1) with fresh f(x), obtaining ¬P(x)∨R(x,f(x)) and ¬P(x)∨P(f(x)). Clause (3) is P(c) for fresh c.
The other clauses are ¬R(u,v)∨Q(u)∨Q(v) and ¬P(z)∨¬Q(z), with variables standardized apart.
Resolve P(c) with the first two clauses using x↦c: obtain R(c,f(c)) and P(f(c)). Resolve (4) at z↦c and z↦f(c) to obtain ¬Q(c) and ¬Q(f(c)).
Resolve the R clause with R(c,f(c)) using {u↦c,v↦f(c)}: obtain Q(c)∨Q(f(c)). Resolving the two negative units gives Q(f(c)) and then □.
A constant for the witness in (1) would incorrectly force the same successor for all P-objects. The fresh constant c and function f have different roles.

extension.prompt: Prove that the four original sentences form a minimally inconsistent theory, using an explicit model after deleting each sentence. steps: Use a singleton {a} for each deletion. Delete (1): P={a},Q=R=∅. Delete (2): P={a},Q=∅,R={(a,a)}. Delete (3): P=Q=R=∅. Delete (4): P=Q={a},R={(a,a)}. Each interpretation satisfies the other three sentences, so every sentence is needed for inconsistency.

exercises.title: A shortest plan with a lower-bound proof
exercises.prompt: Four blocks start with On(A,C), On(C,Table), On(D,B), On(B,Table). Only A and D are clear. The goal is On(A,B), On(B,C), On(C,D). A serial action moves one clear block onto a clear different block or onto the table. Give a shortest plan and prove its length is minimal.
exercises.hint: A must leave C before C moves; it cannot remain on its final support B while B moves.
steps: A five-move plan is: move A from C to Table; move D from B to Table; move C from Table to D; move B from Table to C; move A from Table to B. Every moved block and non-table destination is clear at its action.
The final state contains the three goal On atoms and D on Table.
B must move from Table to C. C must move from Table to D. D must move off B so B can move: at least one action each.
A must leave C before C can move. That first move cannot be its permanent final move onto B, since B must still move and must be clear then. Therefore A needs at least two moves.
The lower bound is 1+1+1+2=5, attained by the displayed plan. Table destinations do not require the table itself to be clear.
exercises.scope: STRIPS, clear-block preconditions, subgoal interference and Sussman anomaly.

extension.prompt: Characterize every shortest plan, not just one. Prove the temporary destination of A and the final destination of D are forced in a five-move plan. Then impose that On(A,B) must first be achieved before On(B,C); determine the new optimum and prove it.
steps: At length five the lower bound is tight: A moves twice, each other block once. D must end on Table because the goal chain A/B/C/D uses every block; placing D on any block in that chain would create a cycle. A’s first destination must be Table: B cannot move with A on it, D cannot move with A on it, and C is A’s starting support.
After A→Table and D→Table, the remaining order is forced: C→D, B→C, A→B. The first two moves commute and are initially possible, so exactly two five-move plans exist.

Under the extra achievement order, A must move onto B, off B before B moves, and onto B again: at least three A moves, plus one each for B,C,D, giving six. D→Table, A→B, A→Table, C→D, B→C, A→B is a legal six-move witness.

exercises.title: Why an extra SAT step can destroy feasibility
exercises.prompt: Use one fluent Open. Action OpenDoor has precondition ¬Open and effect Open; CloseDoor has precondition Open and effect ¬Open. Initially ¬Open; exactly one action is required at every step. Prove that goal Open at horizon H is reachable iff H is odd. Write a horizon-2 refutation argument, then state the precise change that makes feasibility monotone in H.
exercises.hint: Only one action is applicable in each state. Use induction on time rather than enumerating every horizon.
steps: At time 0 Open is false. If false, only OpenDoor is applicable and it makes Open true. If true, only CloseDoor is applicable and it makes Open false. Thus Open_t is true exactly when t is odd, by induction.
At H=2, exactly-one plus preconditions force OpenDoor₀ and CloseDoor₁, so the effect gives ¬Open₂, contradicting the goal Open₂.
At H=1 a plan exists, while H=2 is UNSAT. Feasibility is therefore not monotone for exact-length encodings without idle steps.
Allow zero actions per step with complete persistence constraints, or add a genuine no-op. Any satisfying H-step plan can then be extended by an idle step without changing the final state.

extension.prompt: Encode the complete H-step problem in CNF using Oₜ, oₜ and cₜ for the fluent and two actions. Prove model/plan equivalence. Then replace exactly-one by at-most-one, retaining frames; classify every feasible H and exhibit a false positive if the frames are deleted.
steps: Use ¬O₀ and O_H. For every t<H add oₜ∨cₜ; ¬oₜ∨¬cₜ; ¬oₜ∨¬Oₜ; ¬oₜ∨Oₜ₊₁; ¬cₜ∨Oₜ; ¬cₜ∨¬Oₜ₊₁. Frames are Oₜ∨¬Oₜ₊₁∨oₜ and ¬Oₜ∨Oₜ₊₁∨cₜ.

Any satisfying assignment chooses exactly one applicable action and its next state; conversely every legal exact-length plan satisfies all clauses. The earlier parity argument classifies these models.

After deleting only oₜ∨cₜ, frames make the no-action case persist. Feasibility is now exactly H≥1: open once and idle; H=0 contradicts the initial state. Without frames, at H=1 the assignment O₀=false,O₁=true,o₀=c₀=false satisfies all remaining clauses although no action opened the door.

extension.prompt: Determine every pseudo-intent of this context and its canonical implication basis. Use the definition: P is a pseudo-intent iff P≠P″ and every pseudo-intent Q strictly contained in P has Q″⊆P. Prove the basis generates the listed closure system and that no rule is redundant.
steps: The pseudo-intents are b,c,ad,abc. Sets ∅,a,d,ab,ac,abcd are closed. The remaining nonclosed sets bc,bd,cd,bcd omit a despite containing b or c, and abd,acd contain ad but omit part of ad″=abcd; these fail the recursive condition. The four listed sets pass it.

The canonical basis is b→a, c→a, ad→bc, abc→d. Starting from any subset, these rules reproduce the six closed sets: with no b or c, only ad needs expansion; with b or c, a is added, and having both or also d forces the full set.
Nonredundancy witnesses after removing the respective rules are b, c, ad, abc. Each satisfies the other rules but not the removed rule, so every rule is essential.

exercises.title: From transactions to an implication basis
exercises.prompt: Transactions are abc, abc, ab, ac, bc. At support count at least 2, list all frequent nonempty itemsets and identify the closed and maximal frequent sets. At confidence ≥2/3 list every rule with union abc. Is there any nontrivial exact implication in this context? Justify your final claim using all closed itemsets, including ∅.
exercises.hint: Compute the closure system separately from the frequency threshold. Equality at 2/3 is accepted.
steps: Singletons a,b,c have support count 4 each; ab,ac,bc have count 3 each; abc has count 2. All seven nonempty itemsets are frequent.

All eight subsets including ∅ are closed: no attribute is shared by all transactions, each singleton’s extent has no extra common attribute, each pair lacks the third in one transaction, and abc is already full. All seven nonempty frequent sets are closed; only abc is maximal frequent.
Rules ab⇒c, ac⇒b and bc⇒a have confidence 2/3 and support 2/5, so all meet the threshold. Rules a⇒bc, b⇒ac, c⇒ab have confidence 1/2 and fail.

No nontrivial exact implication X→Y with Y not contained in X holds: X″=X for every X. The empty set of implications is already a complete basis for this closure system, while high-confidence association rules still exist.

extension.prompt: Generalize to n attributes, n≥2. Construct a context with exactly n objects in which every attribute subset is closed. Prove that n objects are necessary for this property, and count the resulting concepts. Explain what duplicating rows can change about association rules while leaving exact implications unchanged.
steps: Let U={a₁,…,aₙ}; object i has U∖{aᵢ}. The objects supporting B are exactly those whose missing attribute is outside B. Intersecting their rows yields B. For B=U the extent is empty and its intent is U by vacuity. Hence every one of the 2ⁿ subsets is closed.

For necessity, each coatom U∖{aᵢ} must be closed. Some supporting object must omit aᵢ, otherwise its closure would include it; that object must therefore have exactly U∖{aᵢ}. These n distinct rows require at least n objects. The construction is optimal.

Duplicating a row does not change which attributes are universally common to supporting objects, so closures and exact implications stay fixed. It changes transaction multiplicities and can change support, confidence and which association rules pass thresholds.
rubric: Construction and proof for all subsets including full U

exercises.title: Solve an entire family of weighted problems
exercises.prompt: Clauses p, ¬p∨q, ¬q have arbitrary strictly positive weights α,β,γ. Derive a formula for the Boolean optimum and characterize the optimal assignments including ties. Prove that the Łukasiewicz relaxation has the same optimum for this particular family, without invoking a numerical optimizer.
exercises.hint: Every Boolean assignment must lose some weight. Split the relaxed square into p≤q and p≥q.
steps: Assignments 00,01,10,11 score β+γ, β, α+γ, α+β. Since α,γ>0, 01 is never optimal. The optimum is α+β+γ−min(α,β,γ).
The optimal Boolean assignments are 00 when α is a minimum weight, 10 when β is a minimum, and 11 when γ is a minimum. Include every tied case.
The relaxed objective is αp+βmin(1,1−p+q)+γ(1−q). It is affine on each triangle p≤q and p≥q. An affine function on either closed triangle attains a maximum at one of its vertices.

The two triangles’ vertices are 00,01,11 and 00,10,11, all Boolean. Hence the continuous optimum equals the Boolean optimum here. Tied edges can contain fractional optima, but cannot improve the value.
This equality is specific to the instance family; it is not a general theorem that relaxed weighted MAX-SAT has no integrality gap.
exercises.scope: Weighted MAX-SAT, Łukasiewicz clause relaxation and piecewise-linear optimization.
exercises.origin: Original challenge · course and lab concepts only

extension.prompt: Now give the four clauses p∨q, p∨¬q, ¬p∨q, ¬p∨¬q arbitrary strictly positive weights w₁,…,w₄. Derive both the Boolean and relaxed optima, characterize all their maximizers, and find the largest possible ratio relaxed optimum / Boolean optimum over such weights.
steps: Each Boolean assignment falsifies exactly one clause, and every clause can be the unique false one. With W=Σwᵢ and m=min wᵢ, the Boolean optimum is W−m; precisely the assignments falsifying a minimum-weight clause are optimal.

The point p=q=1/2 satisfies every relaxed clause to degree 1, giving W. Strict positivity means any relaxed optimum must satisfy all four clauses completely. Their inequalities p+q≥1, p≥q, q≥p, p+q≤1 force that point uniquely. The additive gap is m.
Since m≤W/4, the ratio W/(W−m)≤4/3. Equality holds exactly when all four weights are equal. This is a sharp family-wide bound and contrasts with the preceding three-clause family.
rubric: Weighted Boolean optimum with all ties

exercises.title: Derive the residuum instead of memorizing it
exercises.prompt: For T(a,c)=max(0,a+c−1) on [0,1], prove T(a,c)≤b iff c≤min(1,1−a+b). Deduce the residual implication and compare it with the product S-implication at a=0.8,b=0.3. Explain which property the proof uses about b.
exercises.hint: Because b≥0, max(0,x)≤b is equivalent to x≤b.
steps: Since b≥0, max(0,a+c−1)≤b iff a+c−1≤b, equivalently c≤1−a+b. Together with c≤1, this is exactly c≤min(1,1−a+b).
The admissible c form a closed interval ending at min(1,1−a+b), so the supremum is attained and I_Luk(a,b)=min(1,1−a+b).
At (0.8,0.3), this gives 0.5. Product dual disjunction is S(x,y)=x+y−xy, so the product S-implication S(1−a,b)=0.2+0.3−0.06=0.44.
The initial equivalence would fail for negative b: max(0,x) is always nonnegative. The input range [0,1] is part of the argument, not decoration.
exercises.scope: T-norms, dual conorms, S-implication and residual implication.

extension.prompt: For the product t-norm, derive every pair (a,b) where its S-implication and residual implication coincide. For minimum, give the corresponding equality set. For Łukasiewicz, prove equality everywhere. Include all boundary cases and do not infer equality merely from matching sample values.
steps: Product S-implication is 1−a+ab. If a≤b, the residuum is 1, so equality requires a=0 or b=1. If a>b and a=1, both equal b. If 0<a<1 and a>b, equality with b/a reduces to b=a/(1+a), which indeed satisfies b<a. These cases exhaust the square.
For minimum, when a≤b equality requires a=0 or b=1. When a>b, equality between max(1−a,b) and b requires a+b≥1.
For Łukasiewicz, the dual conorm gives S(1−a,b)=min(1,1−a+b), exactly the residual formula established earlier. Its equality set is the whole unit square.
rubric: Complete product equality locus with algebra

exercises.title: Explain the Church predecessor
exercises.prompt: The lab gives PRED=λn.λf.λx.n(λg.λh.h(g f))(λu.x)(λu.u). Prove it represents predecessor with PRED 0=0. Let F=λg.λh.h(g f), G₀=λu.x and Gₖ₊₁=F Gₖ. Derive Gₖ and evaluate Gₖ I for I=λu.u. Show PRED TWO explicitly.
exercises.hint: First compute G₁ and G₂. For k≥1, the invariant is Gₖ=λh.h(f^(k−1)x).
steps: G₁=F G₀→λh.h(G₀ f)→λh.h(x). G₂→λh.h(G₁ f)→λh.h(f x).
For k≥1, if Gₖ=λh.h(f^(k−1)x), then Gₖ₊₁=λh.h(Gₖ f)→λh.h(f^k x). This proves the invariant by induction, with capture-free substitution.
For n=0, G₀ I→x. For n≥1, Gₙ I→I(f^(n−1)x)→f^(n−1)x. Therefore PRED n=λf.λx.f^max(n−1,0)x.
PRED TWO→λf.λx.G₂ I→λf.λx.I(f x)→λf.λx.f x, which is ONE.
The successor application is delayed inside the continuation h; the special G₀ seed prevents applying f on the first iteration.
