extension.prompt: Using the Church predecessor and zero-test, construct truncated subtraction SUB m n and a test LEQ m n. Prove their specifications for all natural m,n by induction, including zero and oversubtraction. Then derive a Church equality test and prove it cannot return TRUE for distinct numerals.
steps: Define SUB=λm.λn.n PRED m. After k iterations the numeral represents max(m−k,0), proved by induction using the predecessor theorem and PRED ZERO=ZERO. At k=n the result is truncated subtraction.
Let ISZERO=λn.n(λx.FALSE)TRUE. Define LEQ=λm.λn.ISZERO(SUB m n). It returns TRUE iff max(m−n,0)=0, equivalently m≤n, including either argument zero.
Define EQ=λm.λn.AND(LEQ m n)(LEQ n m). The Boolean reductions make it TRUE iff m≤n and n≤m, hence iff m=n. Oversubtraction saturates at zero, so both directed comparisons are needed.

exercises.title: Read a higher-order Church encoding
exercises.prompt: Let E=λm.λn.n m, with Church numerals m,n. Identify the arithmetic operation. Reduce E TWO THREE enough to count applications of f. Explain the n=0 case carefully: compare λx.x with the numeral ONE using β-reduction after supplying f and x. Also explain what λn.n(λx.FALSE)TRUE tests.
exercises.hint: Iterating the function TWO three times doubles the application count three times. Zero iterations returns the identity.
steps: E TWO THREE→THREE TWO→λx.TWO(TWO(TWO x)). Supplying f and then x shows 2³=8 applications of f, so the resulting numeral represents 8. Generally E m n represents m^n under Church arithmetic.
For n=0, ZERO m→λx.x. Applied to f and x this yields f x, the same as ONE f x. Thus it represents ONE extensionally, even though it is not the two-abstraction β-normal form λf.λx.f x.
At m=n=0 this encoding returns ONE as well: the encoding chooses the conventional Church-arithmetic value 0^0=1. It is not a claim about limits of real-valued exponentiation.
For the last term, zero applications of λx.FALSE leave TRUE; any positive numeral applies that constant-FALSE function at least once, yielding FALSE. It is a zero test.

Stopping at the outer λs would leave redexes in its body for positive n, so it would not count normalization to the Church numeral. The result depends on the stated reduction strategy and counting convention.

exercises.title: A family ontology that reasons too far
exercises.prompt: Let isBrotherOf⊑isSiblingOf, with domain(isBrotherOf)=Male. Let isSiblingOf be symmetric and transitive, and Male⊓Female⊑⊥. ABox: isBrotherOf(a,b), Female(b). Is the KB consistent? Which sibling self-edges are entailed? Would making isBrotherOf symmetric preserve consistency? Explain the modelling issue without using Protégé.
exercises.hint: Properties of a superrole do not automatically become properties of its subrole. Symmetry plus transitivity creates self-edges.
steps: The KB is consistent. Infer Male(a) from the brother-role domain, isSiblingOf(a,b) by inclusion and isSiblingOf(b,a) by symmetry. No isBrotherOf(b,a) follows from those axioms.
Transitivity gives isSiblingOf(a,a) and isSiblingOf(b,b). A model can have distinct a,b, Male={a}, Female={b}, brother={(a,b)}, sibling={(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(b,b)}.
If brother itself is symmetric, isBrotherOf(b,a) follows, so domain gives Male(b), clashing with Female(b) and disjointness.

A symmetric transitive role with any edge necessarily contains associated self-edges. If the intended sibling relation excludes self-siblings, that combination of axioms is unsuitable; the shared-parent rule in the lab uses explicit differentFrom instead of expecting these axioms to enforce distinctness.
exercises.scope: Family-ontology lab: role hierarchy, domain, symmetry, transitivity and disjointness.

extension.prompt: For an arbitrary relation R, prove that the least symmetric transitive relation containing R is the union of complete directed relations on the non-isolated connected components of the undirected R-graph (a self-loop counts as non-isolated). Prove the consequence for an irreflexive superrole. Apply it to a chain of four asserted sibling edges.
steps: Symmetry forces every edge in both directions. Along any undirected path, transitivity forces an edge between its endpoints. An incident edge and its reverse force the endpoint self-loops, so every active component becomes a complete directed relation.

Conversely the union of these component-wise complete relations is symmetric, transitive and contains R; isolated vertices without self-loops need no pairs. Thus it is exactly the least such relation. If the superrole is additionally irreflexive, any initial edge is impossible because it forces a self-loop.

For the four-edge chain a−b−c−d−e, all five vertices are in one active component, giving all 25 ordered pairs. This semantic closure is much stronger than an ordinary irreflexive sibling interpretation.
rubric: Necessity by path and self-loop derivations
Sufficiency and leastness including isolated vertices
Irreflexive consequence and complete chain closure

exercises.title: When two existential witnesses must coincide
exercises.prompt: Relative to P⊓Q⊑⊥, is C=∃r.P⊓∃r.Q⊓(≤1 r.⊤) satisfiable? Give a semantic proof. Then examine the two repairs separately: remove the upper bound; or remove disjointness. For each repaired case give a smallest possible model and justify its size.
exercises.hint: Two existential statements may use one witness unless disjointness prevents it; the cardinality restriction then matters.
steps: If x∈C, choose an r-successor y∈P and z∈Q. The ≤1 bound forces y=z. That element is in P⊓Q, forbidden by the TBox; C is unsatisfiable.

Remove the upper bound: two domain elements suffice, not necessarily three. Take domain {x,y}, P={x}, Q={y}, r={(x,x),(x,y)}. Then x has both required successors, and P,Q are disjoint. One element cannot inhabit both nonempty disjoint fillers.
Remove disjointness instead: one element x suffices with P=Q={x} and r={(x,x)}. The one successor satisfies both existentials and the upper bound.

The source is allowed to be its own successor because no irreflexivity restriction was imposed. Requiring distinct names or forbidding self-edges without an axiom would incorrectly inflate the minimum.
rubric: Two-element first repair and lower bound

extension.prompt: Let P₁,…,Pₙ, n≥3, satisfy only consecutive disjointness Pᵢ⊓Pᵢ₊₁⊑⊥, with indices cyclic. A root must have an r-successor in every Pᵢ. Determine the smallest upper bound k on its number of distinct successors that permits a model, for even and odd n. Construct minimum-domain models, allowing the root to be one of its successors.
steps: At least two successors are needed because adjacent nonempty fillers are disjoint. If at most two successors are allowed, every Pᵢ intersects the root’s successor set in a singleton: a two-element intersection would leave no witness for a neighboring filler. Consecutive singleton choices must alternate.

For even n, two successors u,v suffice by alternating their filler memberships; use the root u with edges (u,u),(u,v). For odd n, alternation returns to a conflict at the closing edge, so two are impossible.

For odd n, three successors suffice: alternate u,v for P₁,…,Pₙ₋₁ and assign Pₙ only w. Use root u with edges to u,v,w. Adjacent fillers, including the closing pair, are disjoint. Minimum domain sizes are therefore 2 for even n and 3 for odd n; distinct successors already require that many elements.
rubric: Witness-set argument forces alternation under bound two

exercises.title: Consequence, explosion and the Hilbert vocabulary
exercises.prompt: State the precise definitions of formula, valuation, model, satisfiable, tautology, S⊨X, and S⊢X. Evaluate the slide 14 formula a∨((⊥↑a)↓¬a). Complete slide 19: prove that if S entails every formula then S is unsatisfiable. Instantiate the first two Hilbert axiom schemes on slide 34 to derive A⊃A using modus ponens. Explain soundness versus completeness.
exercises.hint: State the definitions first, then work through the supplied instance. Use the source page to check notation.
steps: An atom or truth constant is a formula; applying a connective to formulas produces a formula. A valuation gives atoms Boolean values and extends recursively using the truth tables. A model of S makes every member true; satisfiability means a model exists; validity means every valuation makes the formula true.
Since ⊥↑a is true, (⊥↑a)↓¬a is false, so the whole formula has exactly the truth value of a.
S⊨X means every model of S satisfies X. S⊢X means a finite derivation in the chosen calculus exists. If S entails everything, it entails ⊥, which no valuation satisfies; hence S has no model.
Hilbert instances: (1) A⊃((A⊃A)⊃A); (2) A⊃(A⊃A); (3) (A⊃((A⊃A)⊃A))⊃((A⊃(A⊃A))⊃(A⊃A)). Modus ponens on (1),(3) and then (2) yields A⊃A.
Soundness is ⊢ implying ⊨; completeness is ⊨ implying ⊢. An axiom scheme admits formula substitutions; an inference rule combines already justified premises.
rubric: Three axiom instances and two modus ponens steps

exercises.title: What completeness means in the two lectures
exercises.prompt: Distinguish consistency, completeness of a theory, completeness of a calculus and decidability. State the scope of the two incompleteness results and explain why they do not contradict completeness of first-order logic. Explain Hilbert’s program, proof checking versus proof search, and constructive versus classical existence using the irrational-power example.
exercises.hint: State the definitions first, then work through the supplied instance. Use the source page to check notation.
steps: Consistency excludes deriving a contradiction. A theory is syntactically complete if it proves P or ¬P for each sentence. A calculus is semantically complete if every logical consequence has a derivation. Decidability asks for a terminating yes/no algorithm.

For consistent effectively axiomatized theories strong enough for arithmetic, incompleteness prevents deciding every arithmetic sentence by proof. Under the usual representability conditions, such a theory cannot prove its own formal consistency. Logical completeness concerns all models of the axioms; a sentence independent of a theory need not hold in all its models.

Hilbert sought a secure formal foundation of mathematics, including consistency and effective reasoning. A proof checker verifies a supplied finite derivation; finding that derivation is a different task. Mathlib supplies reusable formalized definitions and results, rather than making every mathematical question decidable.

Let x=(√2)^(√2). If x is rational choose a=b=√2. Otherwise choose a=x,b=√2, giving a^b=2. Both cases prove existence, but this excluded-middle argument does not select a case or compute its witness. A constructive witness can instead be justified by a separate argument, as in T7.

steps: intersectionOf is C⊓D, C(x)∧D(x); unionOf is C⊔D, C(x)∨D(x); complementOf is ¬C, ¬C(x); oneOf {a,b} is x=a∨x=b. someValuesFrom is ∃R.C, ∃y(R(x,y)∧C(y)); allValuesFrom is ∀R.C, ∀y(R(x,y)→C(y)); hasValue a is ∃R.{a}, equivalently R(x,a).

≥n R.C counts at least n distinct successors satisfying C; ≤n counts at most n; =n is both bounds. Omit C or use ⊤ for unqualified counting. The ≥n FOL expansion introduces n pairwise distinct witnesses; ≤n forbids n+1 pairwise distinct ones.

Domain D: ∃R.⊤⊑D. Range E: ⊤⊑∀R.E. Subproperty: R(x,y)→S(x,y). Inverse: R(x,y)↔S(y,x). Transitive: R(x,y)∧R(y,z)→R(x,z). Symmetric: R(x,y)→R(y,x). Functional: R(x,y)∧R(x,z)→y=z. Inverse-functional: R(y,x)∧R(z,x)→y=z.

R₁∘R₂⊑R₃ abbreviates ∀x,y,z(R₁(x,y)∧R₂(y,z)→R₃(x,z)). Concrete domains supply data values such as numbers and strings. Object properties relate individuals; data properties relate an individual to a data value.

AL has atomic negation, intersection, value restrictions and limited ∃R.⊤. U adds union, E full existentials, C full negation, N unqualified number restrictions. SHOIN and SROIQ(D) name richer families; the slide identifies OWL 2 DL with SROIQ(D). OWL Lite, DL and Full are the earlier dialect names: do not equate them to the three AL extensions.

OWL gives formal ontology semantics on top of RDF/RDFS vocabulary. RDFS already supports basic inferences such as subclass inheritance; OWL adds richer class/property constraints. owl:Thing=⊤, owl:Nothing=⊥; a class extension is its instance set. The semantic subclass predicate is rdfs:subClassOf. An anonymous class is described by an expression rather than a name. SWRL adds rules; SPARQL queries data; inferred and asserted results may differ.

exercises.prompt: Define interpretation 𝕀=(Δᴵ,·ᴵ), concept/role extensions, TBox/ABox and KB model. State every reasoning task on slides 16–19 and reduce them to inconsistency where appropriate. For T={Student⊑Person,Person⊓Robot⊑⊥} and A={Student(ada),Robot(bot)}, retrieve Person instances and realize ada among {⊤,Person,Student,Robot}. Decide whether Person itself is inconsistent.
exercises.hint: State the definitions first, then work through the supplied instance. Use the source page to check notation.
steps: Δᴵ is a nonempty domain; concepts denote subsets, roles binary relations, and individual names elements. A TBox gives universal concept/role axioms, an ABox concept and role assertions. A model satisfies every axiom and assertion.

C is satisfiable relative to T iff some T-model has a nonempty C extension. Subsumption C⊑D means inclusion in every T-model; equivalence means equal extensions; disjointness means empty intersection in all T-models. C is unsatisfiable iff T⊨C⊑⊥; equivalence is mutual subsumption; disjointness is C⊓D⊑⊥.

Subsumption reduces to unsatisfiability of C⊓¬D; equivalence to unsatisfiability of both C⊓¬D and ¬C⊓D; disjointness to unsatisfiability of C⊓D. Concept satisfiability can be checked by adding C(a) for a fresh name to the ABox.

ABox consistency asks for a common T/A model. Instance checking asks whether every such model satisfies C(a), equivalently whether A∪{(¬C)(a)} is inconsistent relative to T. Retrieval lists named individuals entailed to be in C; realization returns their most specific entailed concepts among a given set.

Person retrieval gives ada only; bot cannot be Person because Robot and Person are disjoint. Ada’s most specific entailed listed concept is Student. Person is satisfiable, and the whole KB is consistent: use two distinct elements for ada and bot with Person=Student={ada}, Robot={bot}.

notation.label: Syntax, semantics, alphabet, atom, formula, arity
notation.definition: Syntax specifies well-formed expressions and transformations; semantics gives them meanings. An alphabet supplies atoms, truth constants and connectives. An atom contains no connective; a formula is built inductively. Arity is the number of inputs. In the slide’s syntax bullet, “constants and connectors” should read propositional symbols and constants for atomic formulas.

notation.label: ⊤ / T, ⊥, ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊃, ⊂, ≡, ↑, ↓, ⊅, ⊄
notation.definition: Truth, falsehood, negation, conjunction, disjunction, implication, reverse implication, equivalence, NAND, NOR, nonimplication A∧¬B, and reverse nonimplication ¬A∧B. The slide’s syntactic symbols differ from its semantic Boolean operations. In A⊂B, ⊂ denotes reverse implication; set inclusion elsewhere is a different use.

notation.label: Valuation v:F→{True,False}
notation.definition: A truth assignment to atoms extends recursively to formulas. v(¬A)=Not v(A), and v(A•B) applies the Boolean operation matching •. Evaluating a∨((⊥↑a)↓¬a) yields v(a), because ⊥↑a is true and true NOR anything is false.

notation.label: Model, satisfiability, tautology, SAT, S⊨X, ⊨X
notation.definition: A model satisfies every assumption. Satisfiability asks for at least one such valuation; a tautology holds under all valuations. SAT asks whether a propositional instance has a model (and a solver may return a witness). S⊨X quantifies over models of S; ⊨X denotes validity. S∪{¬X} is inconsistent exactly when S⊨X.

notation.label: Explosion, monotonicity, semantic deduction theorem
notation.definition: An inconsistent premise set entails every formula. Adding premises cannot destroy an entailment. S∪{X}⊨Y iff S⊨X→Y; these claims use universal quantification over models, including an empty model class.

notation.label: Replacement, NNF, CNF, DNF, literal, clause, [], ⟨⟩, □
notation.definition: Replacement of equivalent subformulas preserves truth. NNF puts negations only on atoms; a literal is an atom or its negation. CNF conjoins disjunctive clauses; DNF disjoins conjunctive terms. [...] is generalized disjunction; ⟨...⟩ generalized conjunction. [] or the resolution □ is false; ⟨⟩ is true.

notation.label: Resolution, ⊢, axiom scheme, modus ponens, soundness, completeness
notation.definition: Resolution removes one complementary pivot from two clauses and retains the other literals. S⊢X denotes a syntactic proof. A scheme represents all uniform formula instances. Modus ponens derives Y from X and X→Y. Soundness: derivable implies entailed; completeness: entailed implies derivable. The grandparent rule illustrates matching a rule to ground facts.

notation.label: ∈, ⊆, ∪, ∩, ∅, |S|, iff, ∀, ∃, index i
notation.definition: Membership, subset inclusion, union, intersection, empty set and cardinality are set notation. “iff” is a two-way implication. ∀ and ∃ in a semantic definition quantify over objects such as valuations, rather than becoming propositional connectives. An index labels members of a family; an empty disjunction/conjunction uses the false/true boundary respectively.

notation.label: Signature, constant c, variable x, function f, predicate p, term, atomic formula
notation.definition: A signature specifies symbols and arities. A term is a variable, constant or function applied to terms; a predicate applied to terms is an atomic formula. Terms denote domain elements; formulas have truth values. A closed term has no variables; a closed formula has no free variables.

notation.label: Free/bound occurrence, scope, closed formula, renaming
notation.definition: A quantifier binds occurrences of its variable in its scope. A variable can have both free and bound occurrences in one formula. Renaming a binder requires renaming exactly its bound occurrences and avoiding capture. Prenex transformations require the moved variable to be absent from the other operand’s free variables.

notation.label: M=(D,I), cᴵ, fᴵ:Dⁿ→D, pᴵ⊆Dⁿ, assignment A, tᴵ,ᴬ, attitude
notation.definition: D is a nonempty domain. I interprets constant/function/predicate symbols. A assigns values to variables. Terms are evaluated recursively under I,A; an atomic formula is true when its tuple belongs to the predicate relation. An attitude is the lecture’s term for this truth value.

notation.label: ∀x, ∃x, A[x↦d], truth in a model, validity, satisfiability
notation.definition: Evaluate ∀xF under every replacement d∈D for x; ∃xF needs one. For open formulas, the lecture’s truth-in-model convention quantifies over all assignments; satisfiability needs one shared assignment making all premises true. Validity ranges over every interpretation and assignment.

notation.label: Prenex form, matrix, Skolemization, F(x/f(...)), unifier, substitution
notation.definition: Prenex form has a quantifier prefix and quantifier-free matrix. Skolemization replaces existential witnesses by fresh constants/functions depending on preceding universal variables, preserving satisfiability in an expanded signature. F(x/f(...)) indicates substitution, not division. A unifier makes terms identical; an MGU permits all other unifiers by further substitution.

notation.label: Implicit universal closure, decidable, semidecidable
notation.definition: Clause variables remain universally quantified after the written ∀ symbols are dropped. A decision procedure terminates with either answer on every input. A semidecision procedure guarantees termination for positive instances; first-order validity has complete proof search but no general terminating yes/no procedure.

notation.label: Forward and backward chaining
notation.definition: Forward chaining starts from facts and derives consequences. Backward chaining starts from a goal and recursively seeks premises of rules that conclude it. A failed branch is not by itself a countermodel; a search may need other branches or continue indefinitely.

notation.label: State, STRIPS, action schema, precondition, add/delete effect, goal, plan
notation.definition: STRIPS uses fact sets and parameterized actions. A ground action is applicable when its preconditions hold; its successor is (s∖delete)∪add. Unaffected facts persist. A goal is a condition and may leave many final facts unspecified. A plan is an applicable action sequence reaching a goal state.

notation.label: At, BoxAt, BananaAt, Level, Have, On, Clear, Table; !
notation.definition: At/BoxAt/BananaAt record positions; Level records height and Have possession. On relates a block to its support; Clear means no block is on top; Table identifies the special support. The lecture’s ! means a negative precondition or deleted fact, according to context, not a programming factorial.

notation.label: Sussman anomaly, subgoal interaction, backtracking
notation.definition: Solving interacting goals irreversibly one after another can undo earlier progress. The three-block example requires moving c off a before stacking b on c and a on b. Backtracking revisits choices; cycle control is necessary for finite-state exhaustive search to terminate reliably.

notation.label: Grounding, fluent, time layer, horizon, action mutex, explanatory frame
notation.definition: A fluent is a state-dependent fact. Grounding substitutes object constants; time indices select a state/action layer. H transitions use H+1 state layers. Mutual exclusion forbids simultaneous choices; exactly-one also requires at least one. An explanatory frame requires a cause for each truth-value change. Object/Source/Destination factor a ground move into three selectors.

notation.label: p(s′|s,a), π:s↦a, s —a,r→ s′, γ, E[rₜ], Σₜ γᵗE[rₜ]
notation.definition: p is the transition distribution; π chooses an action for each observed state; r is a transition reward. γ discounts future rewards, t indexes time, E averages over random transitions. The sum is expected discounted return. A plan commits to actions; a policy can react to the reached state. Partial observability means the true state may be hidden; the slides give a state-policy overview only.

notation.label: Knowledge discovery, prepared data, pattern mining, concept hierarchy
notation.definition: The lecture pipeline acquires and prepares data, mines patterns, interprets/evaluates them and represents knowledge for reasoning. FCA extracts concepts and their hierarchy from object/attribute incidence; association mining finds recurring item combinations. Domain knowledge guides this iterative process.

notation.label: K=(X,Y,I), A↑, B↓, extent, intent, Galois connection, C(K), ⪯
notation.definition: X is the object set, Y the attributes, I⊆X×Y incidence. A↑ lists common attributes; B↓ lists matching objects. A concept (A,B) has A↑=B and B↓=A. Concepts are ordered by A₁⊆A₂, equivalently B₂⊆B₁; fewer objects and more attributes means more specific. These antitone derivations form a Galois connection.

notation.label: Closure ↑↓ / ↓↑, 2ˢ, extensive, monotone, idempotent, closed
notation.definition: 2ˢ is the set of subsets of S. A closure cl satisfies A⊆cl(A), A⊆B⇒cl(A)⊆cl(B), and cl(cl(A))=cl(A). The two FCA closures act on object/attribute sets respectively. A set is closed when it equals its closure. Prime/double-prime notation in the other atlas questions denotes the same derivations/closures with the domain determined by the input.

notation.label: Poset, complete lattice, Hasse diagram, ⋀ meet, ⋁ join, infimum/supremum
notation.definition: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. A complete lattice has greatest lower and least upper bounds for every subset. Hasse edges show immediate cover relations, leaving out transitive edges. In the concept lattice meet intersects extents; join intersects intents; the opposite components are obtained by closure of their unions.

notation.label: NextClosure, lectical order, pivot, |X|, |Y|, |C|, O(|X||Y|²|C|)
notation.definition: NextClosure lists all closed intents in an attribute-induced lectical order. At pivot i close (B∩{j:j<i})∪{i}; accept only if no earlier absent attribute appears. Start at cl(∅). |X|,|Y|,|C| count objects, attributes and concepts; the lecture’s bound is output-sensitive because there can be exponentially many concepts.

notation.label: Close-by-One, Titanic, Bordat, Chein, Lindig
notation.definition: At the overview level in the lecture: CbO uses canonicity to avoid duplicate concepts; Titanic uses support and levelwise generation for iceberg lattices; Bordat organizes concept generation with a spanning-tree structure; Chein intersects intents in layers; Lindig generates upper neighbours bottom-up. Their quoted costs depend on |X|,|Y| and output |C|. No implementation of these algorithms is required here.

notation.label: Clarified, reduced, reducible, isomorphic
notation.definition: Clarified means no duplicate rows or columns. Reduced also removes rows/columns derivable as intersections of others. Lattice isomorphism preserves the ordered structure under relabeling. Removing duplicate transactions without preserving multiplicities can change support even if the concept lattice is unchanged.

notation.label: Z₁⇒Z₂, validity, Armstrong, basis, nonredundant, DG basis, pseudo-intent
notation.definition: Validity means Z₁↓⊆Z₂↓. Armstrong’s rules are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. A complete basis derives all valid implications; a nonredundant basis cannot lose a rule. Pseudo-intents P are nonclosed sets whose contained smaller pseudo-intents Q satisfy Q″⊆P. DG uses P⇒P″∖P and minimizes the number of implications.

notation.label: Many-valued context (X,Y,W,I), scaling, pattern structure, iceberg, stability, triadic/polyadic, relational FCA
notation.definition: I⊆X×Y×W includes values W. Scaling turns value conditions into binary attributes; pattern structures generalize attribute descriptions. Iceberg analysis retains concepts meeting a support threshold; stability concerns robustness of a concept under object selection. Triadic/polyadic contexts involve three/more dimensions, while relational FCA includes links between objects. These are overview terms, not additional algorithmic units.

notation.label: Item, itemset, basket/transaction, σ(X), s(X), c(X⇒Y), minSup, minConf, pass, Cₖ, Lₖ
notation.definition: σ counts transactions containing X; s divides by the number of transactions. Rule support is s(X∪Y); confidence is s(X∪Y)/s(X), defined for s(X)>0. Thresholds select frequent sets/strong rules. A pass scans the database once. Cₖ denotes candidate k-itemsets and Lₖ retained frequent ones. Apriori joins then prunes using support anti-monotonicity.

notation.label: FP-tree, header counts, prefix path, conditional pattern base, FP-Growth, FP-max
notation.definition: An FP-tree merges common prefixes after sorting frequent items consistently, retaining counts. A conditional pattern base is the weighted collection of prefixes leading to an item; FP-Growth mines these recursively without Apriori candidate enumeration. FP-max targets maximal frequent itemsets. Closed sets preserve exact support information; maximal sets alone generally do not.

notation.label: PCY, SON, Toivonen, negative border
notation.definition: PCY hashes pairs in a first pass to filter candidates by frequent buckets. SON finds local candidates on chunks and verifies them globally. Toivonen samples, then verifies candidates and the negative border (minimal infrequent itemsets from the sample), retrying when an omitted frequent itemset is detected. The lecture only requests these high-level distinctions.

notation.label: Lift, independence, positive/negative association, co-occurrence
notation.definition: Lift=c(X⇒Y)/s(Y)=s(X∪Y)/(s(X)s(Y)) when denominators are positive. Values above/equal/below 1 indicate positive association/independence/negative association for the empirical events. Here X∪Y is a union of itemsets: containing it is the intersection of their occurrence events, not an event union. Association is not causation.

notation.label: Leverage, conviction, Zhang, Jaccard, certainty, Kulczynski
notation.definition: At the slide’s recognition level: leverage compares observed and independent co-occurrence; conviction measures implication strength through failures; Zhang quantifies association/dissociation; Jaccard measures overlap; certainty expresses the change in consequent probability; Kulczynski averages the two directional conditional probabilities. The slide supplies names and meanings, not six additional numerical formulas to memorize.

notation.label: Crisp truth, fuzzy truth degree, probability, weighted logic, PSL
notation.definition: Crisp truth is Boolean; fuzzy truth models graded membership; probability models uncertainty about an event; weights prioritize formulas. PSL combines soft truth assignments with weighted formula objectives and constraints. Equal numerical values do not make these interpretations interchangeable.

notation.label: Standard negation, Yager negation Nw(x), parameter w
notation.definition: Standard negation is 1−x. Yager negation is (1−x^w)^(1/w), w>0. Both reverse order, exchange 0 and 1, and are involutive; w=1 recovers standard negation.

notation.label: Arithmetic/harmonic mean, t-norm T, monotonicity, associativity, neutrality
notation.definition: Binary means need not associate and generally lack neutral element 1, so they are not t-norms. T:[0,1]²→[0,1] is commutative, associative, monotone and satisfies T(a,1)=a. The lecture’s “non-commutativity” label at the means example concerns non-associativity; these means are commutative.

notation.label: Minimum, product, Łukasiewicz, drastic; weak contradiction
notation.definition: The t-norms are min(a,b), ab, max(0,a+b−1), and the drastic rule b if a=1, a if b=1, otherwise 0. Drastic≤T≤min for every t-norm. Weak contradiction means T(a,1−a)≤1/2, not necessarily 0.

notation.label: Dual t-conorm S or ⊥, maximum, probabilistic/bounded/drastic sum
notation.definition: S(a,b)=1−T(1−a,1−b) has neutral element 0. The four examples are max(a,b), a+b−ab, min(a+b,1), and b if a=0, a if b=0, otherwise 1. The t-conorm symbol ⊥(a,b) is an operation in this deck, not the constant false.

notation.label: S-implication, R-implication / residuum, sup, satisfied implication, I
notation.definition: S-implication is S(1−x,y). Residuum R_T(x,y)=sup{z∈[0,1]:T(z,x)≤y}. For the three continuous t-norms in the lecture, R_T(x,y)=1 iff x≤y. I assigns atoms truth degrees and extends by the selected operators. sup is a least upper bound, not an ordinary maximum without an attainment argument.

notation.label: Interpretation, inference, P₁∧…∧Pₙ⇒φ C, aggregation φ, least solution
notation.definition: Interpretation evaluates a formula at fixed truth values. Positive inference raises variable values above initial lower bounds to satisfy C≥φ(P₁,…,Pₙ), choosing the pointwise least solution. Fair monotone continuous iteration approaches a least fixed point; finite convergence needs more than continuity alone. Negation can destroy monotonicity and feasibility.

notation.label: Universe U, fuzzy set μ:U→[0,1], support, core, α-cut, α-capping
notation.definition: μ(x) is a degree of membership. Support={x:μ(x)>0}; core={x:μ(x)=1}; cutα={x:μ(x)≥α}; capα(x)=min(α,μ(x)). Cuts are crisp sets, caps are fuzzy functions. Intersection/union apply a chosen t-norm/conorm pointwise.

notation.label: Fuzzy equality E:X²→[0,1], T-transitivity, fuzzification
notation.definition: E is symmetric, reflexive with diagonal 1 and satisfies T(E(x,y),E(y,z))≤E(x,z). A crisp set A is fuzzified to μ(x)=sup{E(x,y):y∈A}; in a finite nonempty case this is a maximum.

notation.label: Defuzzification d(μ), first/mean of maxima, median
notation.definition: Defuzzification chooses a crisp output value. First of maxima chooses the smallest maximizing argument; mean of maxima averages maximizing arguments. The slide’s median balances membership mass on either side. Mean and median may land where membership is below its maximum; exact balance need not exist for a finite discrete set.

notation.label: Mamdani system, input pᵢ, fuzzy predicate Pᵢ, firing strength α, output C
notation.definition: Evaluate input memberships Pᵢ(pᵢ), combine them by a t-norm to obtain α, clip the consequent membership C at α, then defuzzify. The HOT/CROWDED example uses min(0.9,0.6)=0.6. Output C is a membership function, while the final c is a crisp fan speed.

notation.label: SAT, MAX-SAT, weighted MAX-SAT, Boolean world, w(c)
notation.definition: SAT asks if all clauses can be true; MAX-SAT maximizes the number satisfied; weighted MAX-SAT maximizes their summed weights. A Boolean world assigns every atom 0 or 1. Hardness of the general problem does not say every instance needs exhaustive enumeration.

notation.label: Relaxation, S atoms / C clauses, y:S→[0,1], positive/negative literals, hinge loss, convexity
notation.definition: Relaxation allows soft truth values. A clause truth is min(sum of its literal values,1), with negative literals contributing 1−y(s). For nonnegative weights, maximizing the concave weighted truth sum equals minimizing the convex weighted loss Σw(c)max(1−sum_literals,0). A hard bound y(s)≤v restricts feasibility.

notation.label: Coordinate-update illustration (“Hit and Run” heading), convergence, potentials
notation.definition: The displayed steps hold all but one variable fixed and improve that coordinate. SZ9 traces exactly that illustration. Its heading is not a proof of a general convergence or polynomial-time guarantee for arbitrary coordinate rules. A potential is a clause-associated penalty; the deck mentions richer PSL potentials and arithmetic constraints without deriving them.

notation.label: Hilbert program, consistency, theory/calculus completeness, decidability, formalization
notation.definition: Consistency means no contradiction; syntactic theory completeness decides every sentence by a proof of it or its negation; calculus completeness derives every semantic consequence. Decidability requires termination on both answers. Formalization makes definitions and proof steps checkable; verification remains relative to those definitions/axioms.

notation.label: First and second incompleteness, arithmetic, effective axiomatization, ZF
notation.definition: The theorems concern consistent effectively axiomatized systems sufficiently strong for arithmetic. Such systems leave some sentences undecided and, under the usual formal conditions, cannot prove their own consistency. ZF names Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory; the lecture cites it as a candidate foundation, not a proved-consistent system.

notation.label: λ-calculus, λx.M, M N, binder, FV, α, β, redex, normal form, strong normalization
notation.definition: λ-calculus builds variables, abstractions and applications. FV lists unbound variables; α renames bound names safely; β substitutes an argument into a function body. A redex has form (λx.M)N. A normal form has no redex; strong normalization requires every reduction sequence to terminate. Untyped Ω reduces to itself.

notation.label: Church numerals, fⁿx, successor, addition, multiplication, Church booleans
notation.definition: Numeral n is λf.λx.fⁿx: fⁿ means n-fold composition, not numeric exponentiation of f. Successor applies f once more; addition composes iterations; multiplication iterates an n-fold map m times. TRUE/FALSE select their first/second argument, enabling NOT, AND and OR.

notation.label: σ, τ, Γ, x:σ, Γ⊢M:τ, function type, natural deduction, discharge
notation.definition: σ,τ denote types; Γ is a context of assumptions or typed variables. x:σ declares a type; Γ⊢M:τ is a typing judgment. Function arrows associate to the right. Introduction builds a connective/proof object, elimination uses it; discharge ends a temporary assumption’s scope.

notation.label: Curry–Howard; →, ∧, ∨, ⊤, ⊥, ∀, ∃ ↔ →, ×, +, 1, 0, dependent product/sum
notation.definition: Propositions correspond to types, proofs to terms. Implication is a function type; conjunction a product; disjunction a sum; truth the unit type; falsehood the empty type. Universals correspond to dependent products and existentials to dependent pairs carrying a witness and proof.

notation.label: Lean / Rocq / Isabelle, Mathlib; Bool, Nat, Type; rfl, rw, intro, exact, apply, induction, by_contra, linarith, ring, simp
notation.definition: Lean, Rocq and Isabelle are proof-assistant systems; Mathlib is a Lean library. Bool is a Boolean type, Nat an inductive natural-number type, Type a universe notation. Tactics construct/check proofs: reflexivity, rewriting, assumption introduction, supplied proof, theorem application, induction, contradiction, linear arithmetic, polynomial normalization and simplification respectively.

notation.label: Constructive witness, classical existence, excluded middle P∨¬P
notation.definition: A constructive existence proof supplies a witness with its justification. The irrational-power argument splits on a proposition without deciding which case holds; excluded middle licenses that classical split.

notation.label: Concept A, role R, individual a, 𝕀=(Δᴵ,·ᴵ), TBox T, ABox A, KB
notation.definition: Concepts denote subsets of a nonempty domain; roles denote binary relations; individuals denote domain elements. The TBox holds terminology axioms; the ABox assertions about individuals. A KB model satisfies both. DL syntax is variable-free but has a translation into FOL; decidability depends on the chosen DL.

notation.label: ⊤, ⊥, ¬, ⊓, ⊔, ∃R.C, ∀R.C, ⊑, ≡, ≥n R.C, ≤n R.C
notation.definition: The constructors denote universal/empty sets, complement, intersection, union, existential successor and all-successor restrictions. C⊑D is inclusion in every model of the TBox; C≡D mutual inclusion. Number restrictions count distinct successors, qualified by C when present. Universal restrictions can hold without successors.

notation.label: AL, ALU, ALE, ALC, ALN, SHOIN, SROIQ(D)
notation.definition: AL supplies atomic negation, conjunction, value restrictions and limited existential restrictions. U adds union, E full existential restriction, C full negation and N unqualified number restrictions. SHOIN and SROIQ(D) name richer languages; SROIQ(D) underlies OWL 2 DL. These names do not license adding unintroduced proof algorithms.

notation.label: Concept satisfiability, subsumption, equivalence, disjointness, ABox consistency, instance check, retrieval, realization
notation.definition: Satisfiability needs a model with a nonempty concept; subsumption is universal inclusion; equivalence universal equality; disjointness universal empty intersection. ABox consistency needs a common model; instance checking tests entailed membership; retrieval returns entailed named instances; realization selects their most specific entailed concepts.

notation.label: Inverse R⁻, transitive, subrole, symmetric, functional, inverse-functional, role chain ∘
notation.definition: Inverse reverses pairs; transitivity composes a relation with itself; subrole is relation inclusion; symmetry adds reversed pairs. Functionality permits at most one successor, inverse functionality at most one predecessor, with equality rather than automatic inconsistency if names coincide. A chain R₁∘R₂ follows two successive edges.

notation.label: Concrete domain, object/data property, nominal {a}, hasValue, anonymous class, extension
notation.definition: Concrete domains provide data values/predicates. Object properties link individuals; data properties link to values. {a} is a singleton concept (nominal); hasValue a is ∃R.{a}. An anonymous class is specified by an expression; its extension is the set of instances.

notation.label: Ontology, formal, explicit, shared conceptualization, taxonomy, knowledge graph, triple
notation.definition: An ontology specifies a community’s domain concepts and constraints in a machine-readable way. A taxonomy is an is-a hierarchy; other relations connect concepts non-taxonomically. Triples represent subject–predicate–object instance data; ontology axioms give vocabulary and support inference.

notation.label: O=(C,R,H_C,rel,A_O), KB=(O,I,inst,instr), dom, range, π₁, π₂, 2ᴵ, L_KB
notation.definition: H_C is the concept hierarchy; rel maps role names to domain/range concept pairs; π₁,π₂ project that pair. A_O contains axioms. I is the individual set; inst maps concepts to subsets of I and instr roles to subsets of I×I. L_KB names a lexicon; the slide does not define the components of its displayed (L_I,J) pair.

notation.label: Top-level/domain/task/application ontology, lightweight/heavyweight, ontology lifecycle
notation.definition: Top-level concepts are generic; domain/task ontologies specialize a field/activity; application ontologies serve a particular use. Lightweight models use simpler structure; heavyweight models richer axioms. The lifecycle covers selection/development, population, validation, evolution, maintenance and deployment.

notation.label: Modus ponens/tollens, detection–choice–execution, metarule, forward/backward/mixed chaining
notation.definition: Modus ponens uses A,A→B to infer B; tollens uses ¬B,A→B to infer ¬A. Detection matches premises, choice selects a rule and execution updates facts. Metarules guide selection. Forward chaining derives from facts; backward chaining seeks premises of a goal; mixed chaining combines these directions.

notation.label: RDF, RDFS, OWL Lite/DL/Full, OWL 2 DL, owl:Thing/Nothing, SWRL, SPARQL
notation.definition: RDF represents triples; RDFS adds basic schema and inference; OWL adds richer logical constraints. Lite/DL/Full are earlier OWL dialects; OWL 2 DL uses SROIQ(D). Thing/Nothing denote ⊤/⊥. SWRL adds rules; SPARQL queries graphs; a reasoner derives consequences. The standard subclass predicate is rdfs:subClassOf.
